To address this we introduce a novel approach to interpretability that looks at the mapping a model learns from sentences to representations as a kind of language in its own right. In doing so we introduce a set of information-theoretic measures that quantify how structured a model's representations are with respect to its input, and when during training that structure arises. Our measures are fast to compute, grounded in linguistic theory, and can predict which models will generalise best based on their representations. We use these measures to describe two distinct phases of training a transformer: an initial phase of in-distribution learning which reduces task loss, then a second stage where representations becoming robust to noise. Generalisation performance begins to increase during this second phase, drawing a link between generalisation and robustness to noise. Finally we look at how model size affects the structure of the representational space, showing that larger models ultimately compress their representations more than their smaller counterparts.

papers.title: Robust Semantic Interpretability: Revisiting Concept Activation Vectors
papers.research_question: How can concept activation vectors be improved to provide more accurate and robust semantic interpretability for image classification models, quantifying concept sensitivity at both the image and dataset levels?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Robust Concept Activation Vectors (RCAV), a method for semantic interpretability that improves upon TCAV by generalizing to non-linear effects and using stricter permutation testing, and introduces two benchmark datasets with metrics for realistic evaluation of semantic interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: RCAV improves upon previous semantic interpretability methods in accuracy, robustness, and runtime, and the introduced benchmarks address a gap in the interpretability evaluation literature.
papers.key_findings:
RCAV accurately quantifies image-level concept sensitivity for both semantically meaningful and confounding concepts, significantly outperforming TCAV which fails at this task.
RCAV reduces the false positive rate to 0% on tested concepts through improved hypothesis testing (permutation test), whereas TCAV exhibits a 100% false positive rate.
RCAV performs robustly across hyperparameters (layer choice, step size) and datasets (TFMNIST, CAMELYON16, ImageNet), though performance drops when concept encoding is non-linear (e.g., in TFMNIST).
The proposed benchmarks (Textured FMNIST and Biased CAMELYON16) provide ground-truth concept sensitivity for realistic evaluation, exposing the importance of counterfactual augmentation and negative controls.
Permutation testing is necessary for robust hypothesis testing in interpretability; the t-test used in TCAV underestimates variance and leads to false positives.
papers.limitation:
RCAV's performance depends on the linearity of concept encoding in the model's latent space; non-linear encodings (as observed in TFMNIST) limit its effectiveness.
RCAV does not account for non-linearity in the initial layers of the model, as it perturbs activations after layer l.
future_direction: Using RCAV to enhance automatic discovery of prediction-relevant concepts.
Conducting a complete comparison of RCAV to other (including non-linear) semantic interpretability methods.
Applying RCAV to scientific discovery, e.g., to assess the importance of specific properties in domains like molecular similarity.
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods for image classification assess model trustworthiness by attempting to expose whether the model is systematically biased or attending to the same cues as a human would. Saliency methods for feature attribution dominate the interpretability literature, but these methods do not address semantic concepts such as the textures, colors, or genders of objects within an image. Our proposed Robust Concept Activation Vectors (RCAV) quantifies the effects of semantic concepts on individual model predictions and on model behavior as a whole. RCAV calculates a concept gradient and takes a gradient ascent step to assess model sensitivity to the given concept. By generalizing previous work on concept activation vectors to account for model non-linearity, and by introducing stricter hypothesis testing, we show that RCAV yields interpretations which are both more accurate at the image level and robust at the dataset level. RCAV, like saliency methods, supports the interpretation of individual predictions. To evaluate the practical use of interpretability methods as debugging tools, and the scientific use of interpretability methods for identifying inductive biases (e.g. texture over shape), we construct two datasets and accompanying metrics for realistic benchmarking of semantic interpretability methods. Our benchmarks expose the importance of counterfactual augmentation and negative controls for quantifying the practical usability of interpretability methods.

papers.title: Mammo-SAE: Interpreting Breast Cancer Concept Learning with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to interpret breast cancer concept learning in a vision-language foundation model, specifically to identify latent neurons associated with clinically relevant concepts and understand the model's decision-making process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mammo-SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework for interpreting breast cancer concept learning in the Mammo-CLIP foundation model, demonstrating that it can identify clinically relevant latent neurons and that finetuning improves concept separation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Mammo-SAE provides a valuable tool for understanding the causal mechanisms within foundation models for medical imaging and opens new avenues for inference-time interventions to improve interpretability and performance in breast cancer detection.
papers.key_findings:
Top-activated class-level latent neurons often align with ground-truth regions of interest, but some neurons respond to confounding background features.
Finetuning Mammo-CLIP leads to larger concept separation in the latent space, improving both interpretability and predictive performance.
SAE-reconstructed features retain most of the original information, with a drop in AUC-ROC of less than 2%.
A small subset of latent neurons (as few as 10) captures most of the task-relevant signal, as shown by intervention experiments.
The model sometimes relies on spurious or task-irrelevant background regions when making predictions, especially in the pretrained variant.
papers.limitation:
Focus exclusively on the final layer of the Mammo-CLIP model, leaving earlier layers unexplored.
Evaluation limited to only two breast cancer-related concepts (mass and suspicious calcification), not extending to other clinically relevant findings.
Analysis confined to Mammo-CLIP; applying the framework to other vision-language models in medical imaging remains for future work.
Visual probing restricted to the top-10 class-level latent neurons per class, which may overlook other relevant neurons.
future_direction: Applying the interpretability framework to other vision-language models in medical imaging, such as MedCLIP or GLoRIA.
Understanding and controlling for background-sensitive neurons to build more robust and interpretable breast cancer detection models.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Interpretability is critical in high-stakes domains such as medical imaging, where understanding model decisions is essential for clinical adoption. In this work, we introduce Sparse Autoencoder (SAE)-based interpretability to breast imaging by analyzing {Mammo-CLIP}, a vision--language foundation model pretrained on large-scale mammogram image--radiology report pairs. We train a patch-level \texttt{Mammo-SAE} on Mammo-CLIP visual features to identify and probe latent neurons associated with clinically relevant breast concepts such as \textit{mass} and \textit{suspicious calcification}. We show that top-activated class-level latent neurons often tend to align with ground-truth regions, and also uncover several confounding factors influencing the model’s decision-making process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that finetuning Mammo-CLIP leads to larger concept separation in the latent space, improving interpretability and predictive performance. Our findings suggest that sparse latent representations offer a powerful lens into the internal behavior of breast foundation models. The code will be released at https://krishnakanthnakka.github.io/MammoSAE/.

papers.title: Discovering Chunks in Neural Embeddings for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Can the cognitive mechanism of chunking be leveraged to interpret high-dimensional neural population activities in artificial neural networks? The paper tests the 'reflection hypothesis' that neural network activities reflect regularities in the data they are trained on.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework that uses the cognitive principle of chunking to identify recurring patterns (chunks) in neural embeddings, showing these chunks reflect data regularities and can causally influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The cognitive tendency for chunking can be leveraged to segment high-dimensional neural activity into recurring, interpretable chunks, revealing a structured reflection of the world within artificial neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
In simple RNNs trained on artificial sequences, hidden states reflect input regularities and can be extracted as interpretable chunks using discrete sequence chunking.
Extracted chunks in RNNs have a causal role: grafting these hidden states alters network predictions and can facilitate compositional learning.
In LLMs (LLaMA3-8B), neural population averaging can extract chunks corresponding to recurring words/concepts, with the extracted subpopulation activity serving as a classifier for the signal.
Unsupervised chunk discovery in LLM embeddings reveals chunks that correlate with abstract concepts like part-of-speech tags, suggesting they capture syntactic information.
The number and diversity of neural population chunks increase with the complexity and hierarchical structure of the input sequence, supporting the reflection hypothesis.
papers.limitation: The approach is an initial proof of concept and has limitations. Future work is needed to test it across different models, establish theoretical foundations, and refine chunk extraction methods.
future_direction: Test the reflection hypothesis across different models.
Establish theoretical foundations for the approach.
Refine chunk extraction methods, such as capturing multi-token chunks in unsupervised discovery.
Extend the framework toward nonparametric chunk discovery.
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging due to their high-dimensional, interacting components. Inspired by human cognition, which processes complex sensory data by chunking it into recurring entities, we propose leveraging this principle to interpret artificial neural population activities. Biological and artificial intelligence share the challenge of learning from structured, naturalistic data, and we hypothesize that the cognitive mechanism of chunking can provide insights into artificial systems. We first demonstrate this concept in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained on artificial sequences with imposed regularities, observing that their hidden states reflect these patterns, which can be extracted as a dictionary of chunks that influence network responses. Extending this to large language models (LLMs) like LLaMA, we identify similar recurring embedding states corresponding to concepts in the input, with perturbations to these states activating or inhibiting the associated concepts. By exploring methods to extract dictionaries of identifiable chunks across neural embeddings of varying complexity, our findings introduce a new framework for interpreting neural networks, framing their population activity as structured reflections of the data they process.

papers.title: Interpretability of artificial neural network models in artificial Intelligence vs. neuroscience
papers.research_question: What are the different notions of interpretability in artificial intelligence and neuroscience, and how can neuroscientific interpretability be pursued independently?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that interpretability in AI and neuroscience are distinct, with neuroscientific interpretability requiring alignment between model components and brain constructs, and proposes that brain alignment can serve as a benchmark for evaluating AI explainability methods.
papers.conclusion: The authors encourage researchers to conceptually separate the objectives of AI and neuroscience interpretability, but suggest that AI interpretability methods aligned with primate brain interpretations are more promising.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a multi-faceted construct used differently in AI (focusing on model component contributions to output) and neuroscience (requiring alignment with brain constructs).
Neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs is relative and depends on the model's intended use and the grain of analysis, with no need for full brain alignment if only specific experimental variables are of interest.
Current ANN models of primate vision contain features not mapped to neuroscientific constructs, limiting their neuroscientific interpretability.
Brain alignment (similarity with primate behavior and neural measurements) can validate the 'goodness' of AI explainability methods in the absence of ground truth.
AI interpretability methods that provide more primate-brain-aligned model interpretations are likely more promising, despite operational differences from brains.
papers.abstract: Computationally explicit hypotheses of brain function derived from machine learning (ML)-based models have recently revolutionized neuroscience. Despite the unprecedented ability of these artificial neural networks (ANNs) to capture responses in biological neural networks (brains), and our full access to all internal model components (unlike the brain), ANNs are often referred to as black-boxes with limited interpretability. Interpretability, however, is a multi-faceted construct that is used differently across fields. In particular, interpretability, or explainability, efforts in Artificial Intelligence (AI) focus on understanding how different model components contribute to its output (i.e., decision making). In contrast, the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs requires explicit alignment between model components and neuroscientific constructs (e.g., different brain areas or phenomena, like recurrence or top-down feedback). Given the widespread calls to improve the interpretability of AI systems, we here highlight these different notions of interpretability and argue that the neuroscientific interpretability of ANNs can be pursued in parallel with, but independently from, the ongoing efforts in AI. Certain ML techniques (e.g., deep dream) can be leveraged in both fields, to ask what stimulus optimally activates the specific model features (feature visualization by optimization), or how different features contribute to the model's output (feature attribution). However, without appropriate brain alignment, certain features will remain uninterpretable to neuroscientists.

papers.title: Capturing Polysemanticity with PRISM: A Multi-Concept Feature Description Framework
papers.research_question: How can we capture polysemanticity (multiple concepts per feature) in large language models to improve automated feature description methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISM, a framework for generating multi-concept feature descriptions that captures polysemanticity in LLMs, outperforming single-concept methods in description quality and faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: PRISM provides a more nuanced and accurate understanding of feature polysemanticity in LLMs, advancing automated interpretability by moving beyond single-concept descriptions.
papers.key_findings:
PRISM (max) achieves higher AUROC and MAD scores than existing feature description methods across multiple models and feature types.
PRISM reveals that individual features often encode a diverse set of concepts, demonstrating polysemanticity.
The degree of polysemanticity varies across model layers and architectures, with no consistent trend with depth.
Neuron-based features (MLP) are generally more interpretable than SAE-based features from the residual stream.
The framework is robust to variations in clustering parameters and the choice of language model for description generation.
papers.limitation: Relies on the quality of clustering and the language model used for description generation, which may produce unfaithful explanations.
future_direction: Extending PRISM to other modalities, such as vision or multimodal models.
Investigating the relationship between polysemanticity and model performance.
papers.abstract: Automated interpretability research aims to identify concepts encoded in neural network features to enhance human understanding of model behavior. Within the context of large language models (LLMs) for natural language processing (NLP), current automated neuron-level feature description methods face two key challenges: limited robustness and the assumption that each neuron encodes a single concept (monosemanticity), despite increasing evidence of polysemanticity. This assumption restricts the expressiveness of feature descriptions and limits their ability to capture the full range of behaviors encoded in model internals. To address this, we introduce Polysemantic FeatuRe Identification and Scoring Method (PRISM), a novel framework specifically designed to capture the complexity of features in LLMs. Unlike approaches that assign a single description per neuron, common in many automated interpretability methods in NLP, PRISM produces more nuanced descriptions that account for both monosemantic and polysemantic behavior. We apply PRISM to LLMs and, through extensive benchmarking against existing methods, demonstrate that our approach produces more accurate and faithful feature descriptions, improving both overall description quality (via a description score) and the ability to capture distinct concepts when polysemanticity is present (via a polysemanticity score).

papers.title: On the Internal Semantics of Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do time-series foundation models internally represent fundamental time-series concepts? Specifically, which layers encode which concepts, are concept parameters linearly recoverable, how do representations evolve in terms of disentanglement and abstraction across depth, and how do models process compositions of concepts?
papers.core_contribution: A systematic probe-based analysis of time-series foundation models reveals that early layers capture local, time-domain patterns while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, and that while atomic concepts are linearly recoverable, representing compositions of concepts remains a challenge.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a structured account of TSFM semantics, showing a layered hierarchy of concept learning and highlighting composition as a key limitation for representing interacting temporal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns such as AR(1) coefficient, trend slope, and level shifts.
Deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals (e.g., variance shifts), with representations becoming more disentangled and abstract with depth.
Spectral and time-warping concepts are the least linearly recoverable from model embeddings.
TSFMs exhibit strong linear compositional properties for most concept pairs, but probe performance degrades for composite concepts, revealing interference.
Representations become more organized and linearly recoverable with increased context length in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
While atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs’ ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.
Spectral and time-warping factors are the least linearly accessible.
future_direction: Explore additional TSFMs, multivariate and irregular datasets.
Adopt controlled-capacity non-linear or causal probes.
Investigate architectures and objectives that better linearize phase and time-warping, and non-linear conditional steering.
papers.abstract: Time-series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have recently emerged as a universal paradigm for learning across diverse temporal domains. However, despite their empirical success, the internal mechanisms by which these models represent fundamental time-series concepts remain poorly understood. In this work, we undertake a systematic investigation of concept interpretability in TSFMs. Specifically, we examine: (i) which layers encode which concepts, (ii) whether concept parameters are linearly recoverable, (iii) how representations evolve in terms of concept disentanglement and abstraction across model depth, and (iv) how models process compositions of concepts. We systematically probe these questions using layer-wise analyses, linear recoverability tests, and representation similarity measures, providing a structured account of TSFM semantics. The resulting insights show that early layers mainly capture local, time-domain patterns (e.g., AR(1), level shifts, trends), while deeper layers encode dispersion and change-time signals, with spectral and warping factors remaining the hardest to recover linearly. In compositional settings, however, probe performance degrades, revealing interference between concepts. This highlights that while atomic concepts are reliably localized, composition remains a challenge, underscoring a key limitation in current TSFMs' ability to represent interacting temporal phenomena.

papers.title: Does TabPFN Understand Causal Structures?
papers.research_question: Does TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, encode causal knowledge in its internal representations beyond statistical correlations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and introduces an adapter framework that can extract this information for causal discovery, outperforming traditional statistical methods.
papers.conclusion: TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, and the proposed adapter framework can extract this information for causal discovery, establishing a new direction for interpretable and adaptable tabular foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Causal information is concentrated in the middle layers (4-6) of TabPFN's encoder.
The proposed framework extracts causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and outperforms statistical baselines (GIES, IGSP, DCDI) on ROC AUC, performing closely to the specialized neural causal discovery model A VICI.
The decoder architecture is crucial for performance; using a learnable decoder significantly improves results compared to using no decoder.
Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, particularly for dense graph structures like Erdős-Rényi and Stochastic Block Model graphs.
Using embeddings from the pre-trained TabPFN encoder (optimal weights) yields better causal discovery performance than using randomly initialized or degraded encoder weights.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades with increasing feature sizes, and the approach is sensitive to the type of graph structure.
future_direction: Leveraging pre-trained tabular models for extracting causal structures and improving their interpretability.
Understanding how tabular foundation models reason about different datasets.
Repurposing tabular foundation models for different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Causal discovery is fundamental for multiple scientific domains, yet extracting causal information from real world data remains a significant challenge. Given the recent success on real data, we investigate whether TabPFN, a transformer-based tabular foundation model pre-trained on synthetic datasets generated from structural causal models, encodes causal information in its internal representations. We develop an adapter framework using a learnable decoder and causal tokens that extract causal signals from TabPFN's frozen embeddings and decode them into adjacency matrices for causal discovery. Our evaluations demonstrate that TabPFN's embeddings contain causal information, outperforming several traditional causal discovery algorithms, with such causal information being concentrated in mid-range layers. These findings establish a new direction for interpretable and adaptable foundation models and demonstrate the potential for leveraging pre-trained tabular models for causal discovery.

papers.title: Decoding Dark Matter: Specialized Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Rare Concepts in Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently capture rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models using sparse autoencoders, without simply scaling the SAE width?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs) for capturing rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models, and demonstrates their effectiveness in capturing tail concepts and improving bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for interpreting foundation models in subdomains, effectively capturing rare concepts and offering practical utility in tasks such as bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
SSAEs capture a greater proportion of tail concepts than standard SAEs trained on general-purpose data.
Dense retrieval is an effective data selection strategy for training SSAEs, outperforming sparse retrieval (BM25).
Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization (TERM) improves concept recall in SAEs, especially for rare concepts, at the cost of some precision.
In a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, SSAEs achieve a 12.5% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when used to remove spurious gender information.
TERM-trained SAEs exhibit stronger activations and lower entropy for tail concepts, making them suitable for rare concept detection.
papers.limitation:
SSAEs require a small seed concept dataset to begin the data selection process.
TERM prioritizes recall, sacrificing some control (precision) for broader concept coverage.
future_direction: Extending SSAEs to other domains and modalities
Applying SSAEs to real-world safety-critical systems
papers.abstract: Understanding and mitigating the potential risks associated with foundation models (FMs) hinges on developing effective interpretability methods. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for disentangling FM representations, but they struggle to capture rare, yet crucial concepts in the data. We introduce Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs), designed to illuminate these elusive dark matter features by focusing on specific subdomains. We present a practical recipe for training SSAEs, demonstrating the efficacy of dense retrieval for data selection and the benefits of Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization as a training objective to improve concept recall. Our evaluation of SSAEs on standard metrics, such as downstream perplexity and $L_0$ sparsity, show that they effectively capture subdomain tail concepts, exceeding the capabilities of general-purpose SAEs. We showcase the practical utility of SSAEs in a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, where SSAEs achieve a 12.5\% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when applied to remove spurious gender information. SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for peering into the inner workings of FMs in subdomains.

papers.title: Prediction is not Explanation: Revisiting the Explanatory Capacity of Mapping Embeddings
papers.research_question: Does prediction accuracy in mapping word embeddings to feature norms reliably indicate genuine feature-based interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that prediction accuracy in property inference methods does not reliably indicate genuine feature-based interpretability, as the results are largely determined by methodological upper bounds and geometric similarity rather than information overlap.
papers.conclusion: Property inference methods do not provide faithful explanations of emergent feature knowledge in word embeddings; instead, they reflect geometric similarities and are limited by methodological constraints.
papers.key_findings:
Property inference methods (PLSR and FFNN) are essentially equivalent when hyperparameters are tuned properly.
The upper bound for perfect information overlap is very low for sparse feature norms, and prediction accuracy is close to this bound.
Random features can be predicted to some degree, and it is not distinguishable whether the result is limited by information overlap or the upper bound.
Corrupting essential linguistic features (like hypernyms) does not significantly change prediction results.
Mapping embeddings to feature norms captures geometric similarity between the matrices, not individual properties.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to three specific feature norms and BERT embeddings.
The study does not explore other property inference algorithms beyond PLSR and FFNN.
future_direction: Analyze the dependence of explanatory power on sparsity, geometric structures, and properties of scores.
Investigate under which circumstances emerging property knowledge could be analyzed with inference methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding what knowledge is implicitly encoded in deep learning models is essential for improving the interpretability of AI systems. This paper examines common methods to explain the knowledge encoded in word embeddings, which are core elements of large language models (LLMs). These methods typically involve mapping embeddings onto collections of human-interpretable semantic features, known as feature norms. Prior work assumes that accurately predicting these semantic features from the word embeddings implies that the embeddings contain the corresponding knowledge. We challenge this assumption by demonstrating that prediction accuracy alone does not reliably indicate genuine feature-based interpretability. We show that these methods can successfully predict even random information, concluding that the results are predominantly determined by an algorithmic upper bound rather than meaningful semantic representation in the word embeddings. Consequently, comparisons between datasets based solely on prediction performance do not reliably indicate which dataset is better captured by the word embeddings. Our analysis illustrates that such mappings primarily reflect geometric similarity within vector spaces rather than indicating the genuine emergence of semantic properties.

papers.title: Understanding Generative AI Content with Embedding Models
papers.research_question: Can embedding vectors from foundation models reveal semantic distinctions in data, particularly separability between real and AI-generated samples?
papers.core_contribution: Embedding vectors from foundation models, when combined with dimensionality reduction, can separate real and AI-generated data, revealing inherent biases (generative DNA) in generative models.
papers.conclusion: Feature embedders can reveal statistical biases in generative models and provide a foundation for automated detection of AI-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
Embedding vectors from feature embedders (FEs) can separate data from different sources, including real vs. AI-generated.
The separability is due to differences in sampling techniques and generative model biases (generative DNA).
Even after normalization (e.g., translation), differences persist due to content and style.
Simple classifiers like Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) achieve high accuracy in distinguishing real and AI-generated data.
The signal in embedded data is low-dimensional, explaining why distributional shifts are easily detectable.
papers.limitation: For short text samples (e.g., one sentence), it is difficult to distinguish between human and machine translations.
papers.abstract: Constructing high-quality features is critical to any quantitative data analysis. While feature engineering was historically addressed by carefully hand-crafting data representations based on domain expertise, deep neural networks (DNNs) now offer a radically different approach. DNNs implicitly engineer features by transforming their input data into hidden feature vectors called embeddings. For embedding vectors produced by foundation models -- which are trained to be useful across many contexts -- we demonstrate that simple and well-studied dimensionality-reduction techniques such as Principal Component Analysis uncover inherent heterogeneity in input data concordant with human-understandable explanations. Of the many applications for this framework, we find empirical evidence that there is intrinsic separability between real samples and those generated by artificial intelligence (AI).

papers.title: Decompose the model: Mechanistic interpretability in image models with Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG)
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability be achieved in image models by systematically tracing the pathway from input to output across an entire dataset, moving beyond class-specific explanations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel approach for mechanistic interpretability in image models, using Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors, and a new Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method to trace their causal contributions across layers for a dataset-wide analysis.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach for extracting and attributing concepts within image models, enabling a comprehensive layer-wise analysis that advances mechanistic interpretability by moving from class-specific to dataset-wide explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The method can extract and attribute 'shared concepts' that are common across similar classes, unlike class-specific explanation methods.
The proposed concept extraction method using bisecting k-means clustering outperforms other methods (like Sparse AutoEncoder and dictionary learning) in fidelity metrics (C-Deletion and C-Insertion) across most layers.
The Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG) method effectively quantifies the causal relationships between concept vectors across different layers, validated by inter-layer deletion/insertion experiments.
The approach provides a holistic, dataset-wide understanding of model behavior, tracing how concepts are constructed and aggregated from lower to higher layers.
future_direction: Extending the method to other deep learning architectures, such as Transformer models.
More thoroughly investigating the implications of analyzing entire datasets rather than focusing solely on class-specific explanations.
papers.abstract: In the field of eXplainable AI (XAI) in language models, the progression from local explanations of individual decisions to global explanations with high-level concepts has laid the groundwork for mechanistic interpretability, which aims to decode the exact operations. However, this paradigm has not been adequately explored in image models, where existing methods have primarily focused on class-specific interpretations. This paper introduces a novel approach to systematically trace the entire pathway from input through all intermediate layers to the final output within the whole dataset. We utilize Pointwise Feature Vectors (PFVs) and Effective Receptive Fields (ERFs) to decompose model embeddings into interpretable Concept Vectors. Then, we calculate the relevance between concept vectors with our Generalized Integrated Gradients (GIG), enabling a comprehensive, dataset-wide analysis of model behavior. We validate our method of concept extraction and concept attribution in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Our approach advances the understanding of semantic significance within image models, offering a holistic view of their operational mechanics.

papers.title: Enhancing Interpretability of Sparse Latent Representations with Class Information
papers.research_question: How can latent space interpretability be enhanced by ensuring that active dimensions in the latent space are consistent across samples within the same class, thereby capturing both global and class-specific factors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel loss function for Variational Sparse Coding that aligns active latent dimensions across samples within the same class, enhancing interpretability by capturing both global and class-specific factors in the latent space.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method enhances latent space interpretability by capturing both global and class-specific features, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the latent space, especially in datasets where global attributes are not uniformly present.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method successfully aligns active latent dimensions within each class, creating a more structured and interpretable latent space.
The method captures global features (e.g., digit thickness and rotation in MNIST) that are shared across all classes.
The method also captures class-specific features (e.g., intersection point in digits 4 and 9, heel prominence in footwear classes in Fashion-MNIST).
Classes within the same category (e.g., boots, sandals, sneakers) share more common active dimensions, indicating stronger latent similarities.
Quantitative analysis using distance metrics (Pearson correlation, Cosine, Euclidean) confirms higher similarity between gamma vectors of classes within the same category.
papers.abstract: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are powerful generative models for learning latent representations. Standard VAEs generate dispersed and unstructured latent spaces by utilizing all dimensions, which limits their interpretability, especially in high-dimensional spaces. To address this challenge, Variational Sparse Coding (VSC) introduces a spike-and-slab prior distribution, resulting in sparse latent representations for each input. These sparse representations, characterized by a limited number of active dimensions, are inherently more interpretable. Despite this advantage, VSC falls short in providing structured interpretations across samples within the same class. Intuitively, samples from the same class are expected to share similar attributes while allowing for variations in those attributes. This expectation should manifest as consistent patterns of active dimensions in their latent representations, but VSC does not enforce such consistency. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to enhance the latent space interpretability by ensuring that the active dimensions in the latent space are consistent across samples within the same class. To achieve this, we introduce a new loss function that encourages samples from the same class to share similar active dimensions. This alignment creates a more structured and interpretable latent space, where each shared dimension corresponds to a high-level concept, or "factor." Unlike existing disentanglement-based methods that primarily focus on global factors shared across all classes, our method captures both global and class-specific factors, thereby enhancing the utility and interpretability of latent representations.

papers.title: LAVA: Explainability for Unsupervised Latent Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we explain the organization of latent embeddings from unsupervised models by relating input features to the structure of the embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LA V A, a post-hoc model-agnostic method that explains unsupervised latent embeddings by extracting modules of feature covariation that reoccur across local neighborhoods in the embedding space.
papers.conclusion: LA V A offers a stable and effective approach for explaining unsupervised latent embeddings, revealing interpretable patterns of feature covariation that are missed by existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
LA V A provides stable explanations across different locality placements and module extraction runs.
LA V A modules capture globally reoccurring local subpatterns of feature correlation, not averaged patterns.
The method reveals domain-relevant patterns, such as visual parts in MNIST and disease-related gene expression in kidney cells.
LA V A outperforms the label-free explainability framework in capturing meaningful local structure.
papers.abstract: Unsupervised black-box models are drivers of scientific discovery, yet are difficult to interpret, as their output is often a multidimensional embedding rather than a well-defined target. While explainability for supervised learning uncovers how input features contribute to predictions, its unsupervised counterpart should relate input features to the structure of the learned embeddings. However, adaptations of supervised model explainability for unsupervised learning provide either single-sample or dataset-summary explanations, remaining too fine-grained or reductive to be meaningful, and cannot explain embeddings without mapping functions. To bridge this gap, we propose LAVA, a post-hoc model-agnostic method to explain local embedding organization through feature covariation in the original input data. LAVA explanations comprise modules, capturing local subpatterns of input feature correlation that reoccur globally across the embeddings. LAVA delivers stable explanations at a desired level of granularity, revealing domain-relevant patterns such as visual parts of images or disease signals in cellular processes, otherwise missed by existing methods.

papers.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies the emergence of interpretable categorical features within large language models (LLMs), analyzing their behavior across training checkpoints (time), transformer layers (space), and varying model sizes (scale). Using sparse autoencoders for mechanistic interpretability, we identify when and where specific semantic concepts emerge within neural activations. Results indicate clear temporal and scale-specific thresholds for feature emergence across multiple domains. Notably, spatial analysis reveals unexpected semantic reactivation, with early-layer features re-emerging at later layers, challenging standard assumptions about representational dynamics in transformer models.

papers.title: A Survey on Mechanistic Interpretability for Multi-Modal Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can LLM interpretability methods be adapted to multimodal foundation models, and what are the mechanistic differences between unimodal and multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive survey of mechanistic interpretability for multimodal foundation models, introducing a taxonomy and comparing insights between unimodal and multimodal models to highlight research gaps.
papers.conclusion: The survey reviews mechanistic understanding methods for MMFMs, introduces a taxonomy differentiating interpretability methods adapted from language models and those designed for multimodal models, and compares mechanistic insights to identify gaps and their impact on downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-based interpretability methods can be extended to MMFMs with moderate adjustments, particularly when treating visual and textual inputs similarly.
Novel multimodal challenges arise such as interpreting visual embeddings in human-understandable terms, necessitating new dedicated analysis methods.
While interpretability aids downstream tasks, applications like hallucination mitigation and model editing remain underdeveloped in multimodal models compared to language models.
There is a substantial gap between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs, with a lack of unified benchmarks and tools for multimodal interpretability.
The survey proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy for mechanistic interpretability in multimodal models based on model family, interpretability techniques, and applications.
papers.limitation:
The survey mainly focuses on image-text multimodal models without considering other modalities such as video, time series, or 3D.
The survey does not contain experimental analysis because of the lack of unified benchmarks.
The survey only focuses on transformer-based or diffusion models, without considering novel model architectures such as MAMBA.
future_direction: Extending mechanistic interpretability techniques to analyze unified vision-text understanding and generation models.
Developing sequential batch model editing techniques for multimodal models, including diffusion and multimodal language models.
Exploring the effectiveness of sparse autoencoders and their variants for controlling and steering multimodal models.
papers.abstract: The rise of foundation models has transformed machine learning research, prompting efforts to uncover their inner workings and develop more efficient and reliable applications for better control. While significant progress has been made in interpreting Large Language Models (LLMs), multimodal foundation models (MMFMs) - such as contrastive vision-language models, generative vision-language models, and text-to-image models - pose unique interpretability challenges beyond unimodal frameworks. Despite initial studies, a substantial gap remains between the interpretability of LLMs and MMFMs. This survey explores two key aspects: (1) the adaptation of LLM interpretability methods to multimodal models and (2) understanding the mechanistic differences between unimodal language models and crossmodal systems. By systematically reviewing current MMFM analysis techniques, we propose a structured taxonomy of interpretability methods, compare insights across unimodal and multimodal architectures, and highlight critical research gaps.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Beyond linear regression: mapping models in cognitive neuroscience should align with research goals
papers.research_question: How should cognitive neuroscientists choose between linear and nonlinear mapping models for relating features to neural data, and does the linear/nonlinear dichotomy adequately capture the relevant considerations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the choice between linear and nonlinear mapping models in cognitive neuroscience should be guided by specific research goals and the complexity of the model, rather than a categorical preference for linearity. It shows that common desiderata like predictive accuracy, interpretability, and biological plausibility each encompass multiple goals with distinct implications for model choice.
papers.conclusion: Researchers should move beyond the linear/nonlinear dichotomy and instead select mapping models by explicitly considering their research goals and the complexity of the model, using complexity metrics to guide evaluation and comparison.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive accuracy, interpretability, and biological plausibility are three overarching desiderata for mapping models, but each corresponds to multiple specific research goals that impose different constraints on the model.
The linear/nonlinear dichotomy is an oversimplification; model complexity is a more informative dimension for selecting mapping models based on research goals.
Linear mapping models are not universally superior for interpretability; interpretability can be defined at different levels (individual weights, representational spaces, feature set description) with varying constraints.
Biological plausibility arguments for linear readout are limited and may not reflect actual neural readout mechanisms, which can be sparse and nonlinear.
Practical considerations like dataset size and measurement properties also influence the feasibility and performance of different mapping model classes.
future_direction: Develop and apply complexity metrics to evaluate mapping models in cognitive neuroscience.
Conduct systematic examinations of how dataset size and measurement properties influence the performance of different mapping model classes.
Further research on neural readout mechanisms to better inform biologically plausible mapping model constraints.
papers.abstract: Many cognitive neuroscience studies use large feature sets to predict and interpret brain activity patterns. Feature sets take many forms, from human stimulus annotations to representations in deep neural networks. Of crucial importance in all these studies is the mapping model, which defines the space of possible relationships between features and neural data. Until recently, most encoding and decoding studies have used linear mapping models. Increasing availability of large datasets and computing resources has recently allowed some researchers to employ more flexible nonlinear mapping models; however, the question of whether nonlinear mapping models can yield meaningful scientific insights remains debated. Here, we discuss the choice of a mapping model in the context of three overarching desiderata: predictive accuracy, interpretability, and biological plausibility. We show that these desiderata do not map cleanly onto the linear/nonlinear divide; instead, each desideratum can refer to multiple research goals, each of which imposes its own constraints on the mapping model. Moreover, we argue that, instead of categorically treating the mapping models as linear or nonlinear, researchers should report the complexity of these models. We show that, in many cases, complexity provides a more accurate reflection of restrictions imposed by various research goals and outline several complexity metrics that can be used to effectively evaluate mapping models.

papers.title: RAVEL: Evaluating Interpretability Methods on Disentangling Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent can different interpretability methods successfully disentangle the roles of neurons in representing multiple high-level concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the RAVEL benchmark for evaluating interpretability methods on attribute disentanglement in language models, and proposes Multi-task Distributed Alignment Search (MDAS) which achieves state-of-the-art results, demonstrating the importance of distributed feature identification.
papers.conclusion: Presents the RAVEL benchmark for evaluating interpretability methods on attribute disentanglement, shows that Multi-task DAS achieves the best results, and releases the benchmark to drive future development of interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Methods with counterfactual supervision (DBM, DAS, MDAS) achieve strong disentanglement scores, while unsupervised featurizers (PCA, SAE) struggle.
Multi-task supervision (MDBM, MDAS) improves isolation of attributes compared to single-task versions.
Some attribute pairs (e.g., country-language, latitude-longitude) are inherently difficult to disentangle in the model.
Attributes become gradually disentangled across transformer layers, with later layers showing higher disentanglement scores.
papers.limitation:
Results are based on Llama2-7B; different model architectures or training paradigms might favor different interpretability methods.
Intervention sites are limited to the residual stream at the last entity token, but attribute representations could be distributed across multiple tokens or layers.
future_direction: Instantiate RAVEL on new models to evaluate interpretability methods.
Explore different intervention sites beyond the residual stream at the last entity token.
papers.abstract: Individual neurons participate in the representation of multiple high-level concepts. To what extent can different interpretability methods successfully disentangle these roles? To help address this question, we introduce RAVEL (Resolving Attribute-Value Entanglements in Language Models), a dataset that enables tightly controlled, quantitative comparisons between a variety of existing interpretability methods. We use the resulting conceptual framework to define the new method of Multi-task Distributed Alignment Search (MDAS), which allows us to find distributed representations satisfying multiple causal criteria. With Llama2-7B as the target language model, MDAS achieves state-of-the-art results on RAVEL, demonstrating the importance of going beyond neuron-level analyses to identify features distributed across activations. We release our benchmark at https://github.com/explanare/ravel.

papers.title: Sparse Concept Anchoring for Interpretable and Controllable Neural Representations
papers.research_question: Can we establish predictable concept locations in a model's latent space during training using minimal supervision, to enable interpretable and controllable representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Concept Anchoring, a framework that uses minimal supervision during training to anchor specific concepts to predetermined locations in latent space, enabling reversible behavioral steering and permanent concept removal via geometric interventions.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Concept Anchoring inverts traditional interpretability by establishing predictable geometric structure during training through minimal supervision, enabling direct interventions on model behavior with minimal collateral impact.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Concept Anchoring organizes latent space predictably using labels for <0.1% of training examples per concept.
The anchored geometry enables reversible behavioral steering (suppression) and permanent concept removal (weight ablation) with high selectivity.
Experiments on color autoencoders show suppression increases reconstruction error for targeted concepts (e.g., red) while preserving orthogonal colors, with error approaching theoretical bounds.
Weight ablation can completely eliminate a concept while preserving orthogonal colors, but requires additional repulsion regularization to isolate the concept.
The method extends to multidimensional concepts (e.g., hue subspace) and works with a single organizational regularizer.
papers.limitation:
Ablation may leave structural traces that could aid adversarial recovery.
Extension to linguistic domains is challenging due to higher-dimensional manifolds, context-dependent similarity, and subjective labeling.
future_direction: Validating SCA in larger models (e.g., GPT-2-scale transformers) and exploring more abstract concepts.
Applying geometric regularization to transformers and considering where to add constraints (e.g., at which layers of the residual stream).
Exploring weak subspace anchoring for fuzzy concepts to reduce the post-hoc search space.
papers.abstract: We introduce Sparse Concept Anchoring, a method that biases latent space to position a targeted subset of concepts while allowing others to self-organize, using only minimal supervision (labels for <0.1% of examples per anchored concept). Training combines activation normalization, a separation regularizer, and anchor or subspace regularizers that attract rare labeled examples to predefined directions or axis-aligned subspaces. The anchored geometry enables two practical interventions: reversible behavioral steering that projects out a concept's latent component at inference, and permanent removal via targeted weight ablation of anchored dimensions. Experiments on structured autoencoders show selective attenuation of targeted concepts with negligible impact on orthogonal features, and complete elimination with reconstruction error approaching theoretical bounds. Sparse Concept Anchoring therefore provides a practical pathway to interpretable, steerable behavior in learned representations.

papers.title: BILLY: Steering Large Language Models via Merging Persona Vectors for Creative Generation
papers.research_question: Without relying on multiple models carrying on a multi-round discussion, can a single LLM simulate diverse perspectives in an efficient manner?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes BILLY, a training-free framework that blends multiple persona vectors in a single LLM's activation space to enhance creativity, outperforming multi-LLM approaches with lower computational cost.
papers.conclusion: BILLY enables efficient and interpretable enhancement of LLM creativity by steering models with merged persona vectors, offering a cost-effective alternative to multi-LLM systems.
papers.key_findings:
BILLY achieves higher originality scores compared to single-model prompting and multi-LLM methods across creativity benchmarks.
BILLY reduces token cost and inference time by over 95% compared to multi-LLM frameworks.
The method allows interpretable control over generation through persona vector blending.
papers.abstract: Multi-LLM systems enhance the creativity of large language models by simulating human collective intelligence but suffer from significant drawbacks, such as high computational costs and inference latency. To address these limitations, we propose BILLY (BlendIng persona vectors for Large Language model creativitY), a training-free framework that captures the benefits of multi-LLM collaboration, i.e. inducing diverse perspectives and specialized expertise, within a single model. BILLY operates by extracting and blending multiple distinct persona vectors directly in the model's activation space. We steer the model's generation process with this merged vector while inference, enabling multi-perspective output without explicit multi-LLM communication. Our experiments across creativity-oriented benchmarks demonstrate that BILLY surpasses single model prompting and traditional multi-LLM approaches, while substantially reducing inference time and computational costs. Our analyses further reveal that distinct persona vectors can be blended to achieve both effective control over complementary aspects of generation and greater interpretability.

papers.title: Interpretability is in the Mind of the Beholder: A Causal Framework for Human-interpretable Representation Learning
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable representations that are aligned with a human's concept vocabulary to enable effective communication between machine and human?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a causal framework for human-interpretable representation learning that formalizes the human element and defines alignment between machine and human concepts as a key requirement for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that alignment is essential for interpretability and that the proposed causal framework establishes a foundation for future research on human-interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment between machine and human representations is a key requirement for interpretability, and it is linked to disentanglement.
Concept leakage, where information from one concept leaks into another, is a result of misalignment and lack of disentanglement.
The framework connects alignment to causal abstractions, ensuring consistency under interventions.
Perfect alignment is not strictly necessary for interpretability; approximate alignment suffices.
The framework provides a foundation for future work on human-interpretable representations.
papers.limitation:
Perfect alignment is not strictly necessary for interpretability, and approximate alignment may suffice.
Alignment alone is not sufficient for successful communication due to factors like human inattention or poor presentation of explanations.
The framework assumes access to the human's concept vocabulary, which may be difficult to obtain in practice.
future_direction: How to measure alignment in practice.
How to implement alignment in representation learning.
How to collect the necessary concept annotations.
papers.abstract: Focus in Explainable AI is shifting from explanations defined in terms of low-level elements, such as input features, to explanations encoded in terms of interpretable concepts learned from data. How to reliably acquire such concepts is, however, still fundamentally unclear. An agreed-upon notion of concept interpretability is missing, with the result that concepts used by both post-hoc explainers and concept-based neural networks are acquired through a variety of mutually incompatible strategies. Critically, most of these neglect the human side of the problem: a representation is understandable only insofar as it can be understood by the human at the receiving end. The key challenge in Human-interpretable Representation Learning (HRL) is how to model and operationalize this human element. In this work, we propose a mathematical framework for acquiring interpretable representations suitable for both post-hoc explainers and concept-based neural networks. Our formalization of HRL builds on recent advances in causal representation learning and explicitly models a human stakeholder as an external observer. This allows us to derive a principled notion of alignment between the machine representation and the vocabulary of concepts understood by the human. In doing so, we link alignment and interpretability through a simple and intuitive name transfer game, and clarify the relationship between alignment and a well-known property of representations, namely disentanglment. We also show that alignment is linked to the issue of undesirable correlations among concepts, also known as concept leakage, and to content-style separation, all through a general information-theoretic reformulation of these properties. Our conceptualization aims to bridge the gap between the human and algorithmic sides of interpretability and establish a stepping stone for new research on human-interpretable representations.

papers.title: Metric Learning Encoding Models: A Multivariate Framework for Interpreting Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural representations by learning a metric over theoretical features that matches the geometry of the neural space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Metric Learning Encoding Models (MLEMs), a multivariate encoding framework that learns a metric over theoretical features to match the geometry of neural representations, enabling modeling of feature interactions and robust feature importance estimation.
papers.conclusion: MLEM provides a versatile and robust tool for interpreting high-dimensional neural representations by modeling the geometry of the feature space to match the neural geometry, applicable across modalities in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
MLEM recovers ground-truth feature weights more accurately than the FR-RSA-I baseline in synthetic simulations.
MLEM is more robust to noise in neural representations compared to FR-RSA-I.
MLEM converges faster during training than FR-RSA-I.
MLEM identifies similar feature importance profiles as FR-RSA-I on real language data but with greater stability.
The symmetric positive definite constraint on the weight matrix provides regularization, leading to improved accuracy and robustness.
papers.limitation:
For very large and heterogeneous datasets, the subsampling strategy may miss informative stimulus pairs related to sparse features, potentially biasing the learned metric.
The framework does not weight individual neural units, which could improve alignment but at the cost of interpretability.
future_direction: Applying MLEM to human brain data (fMRI, MEG, ECoG) to bridge computational models and biological neural computation.
Using MLEM to interpret internal representations of deep learning models across various modalities.
Leveraging MLEM's ability to uncover hierarchical clustering for discovering interpretable structure in high-dimensional representations.
papers.abstract: Understanding how explicit theoretical features are encoded in opaque neural systems is a central challenge now common to neuroscience and AI. We introduce Metric Learning Encoding Models (MLEMs) to address this challenge most directly as a metric learning problem: we fit the distance in the space of theoretical features to match the distance in neural space. Our framework improves on univariate encoding and decoding methods by building on second-order isomorphism methods, such as Representational Similarity Analysis, and extends them by learning a metric that efficiently models feature as well as interactions between them. The effectiveness of MLEM is validated through two sets of simulations. First, MLEMs recover ground-truth importance features in synthetic datasets better than state-of-the-art methods, such as Feature Reweighted RSA (FR-RSA). Second, we deploy MLEMs on real language data, where they show stronger robustness to noise in calculating the importance of linguistic features (gender, tense, etc.). MLEMs are applicable to any domains where theoretical features can be identified, such as language, vision, audition, etc. We release optimized code applicable to measure feature importance in the representations of any artificial neural networks or empirical neural data at https://github.com/LouisJalouzot/MLEM.

papers.title: FADE: Why Bad Descriptions Happen to Good Features
papers.research_question: How to develop a scalable, model-agnostic framework for automatically evaluating feature-to-description alignment in automated interpretability pipelines?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FADE, a framework for evaluating feature-to-description alignment with four metrics, and provides insights into challenges in automated interpretability.
papers.conclusion: FADE provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for feature descriptions, highlighting fundamental challenges in automated interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
FADE identifies limitations of single-metric approaches like simulated-activation-based metrics.
Larger evaluating LLMs yield better evaluations, with models like GPT-4o mini performing well.
Generating feature descriptions for SAEs is more challenging than for MLP neurons.
Interpreting larger SAEs is more difficult due to finer-grained concept decomposition.
Interpretability varies across layers, with some layers like layer 12 in Gemma-2-2b being less interpretable.
papers.limitation: The framework relies on assumptions such as binary concept expression, concept sparsity, feature reactivity, and causality, which may not always hold.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have highlighted the potential of automating interpretability pipelines in analyzing the latent representations within LLMs. While this may enhance our understanding of internal mechanisms, the field lacks standardized evaluation methods for assessing the validity of discovered features. We attempt to bridge this gap by introducing FADE: Feature Alignment to Description Evaluation, a scalable model-agnostic framework for automatically evaluating feature-to-description alignment. FADE evaluates alignment across four key metrics - Clarity, Responsiveness, Purity, and Faithfulness - and systematically quantifies the causes of the misalignment between features and their descriptions. We apply FADE to analyze existing open-source feature descriptions and assess key components of automated interpretability pipelines, aiming to enhance the quality of descriptions. Our findings highlight fundamental challenges in generating feature descriptions, particularly for SAEs compared to MLP neurons, providing insights into the limitations and future directions of automated interpretability. We release FADE as an open-source package at: https://github.com/brunibrun/FADE

papers.title: Decomposing Representation Space into Interpretable Subspaces with Unsupervised Learning
papers.research_question: Can we find interpretable subspaces in neural representations in an unsupervised way? To what extent are different aspects organized in separate subspaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method (NDM) to decompose representation space into interpretable subspaces, showing that these subspaces align with known circuit variables and can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis.
papers.conclusion: Unsupervised decomposition of representation space into interpretable subspaces is possible, and these subspaces can serve as new basic units for circuit analysis, offering a new perspective on understanding model internals.
papers.key_findings:
NDM can find interpretable subspaces without supervision, as shown in toy models and real language models.
Subspaces found by NDM align with variables in known circuits in GPT-2, as evidenced by high Gini coefficients in subspace patching experiments.
The method scales to 2B models, finding separate subspaces for context and parametric knowledge routing.
Qualitative analysis shows that subspaces are consistent and interpretable across different inputs.
papers.limitation: The method can get stuck in local minima, leading to sub-optimal subspace partitions.
future_direction: hierarchical structure of subspaces
more flexible searching over dimension configurations
applying the method to larger models and more tasks
papers.abstract: Understanding internal representations of neural models is a core interest of mechanistic interpretability. Due to its large dimensionality, the representation space can encode various aspects about inputs. To what extent are different aspects organized and encoded in separate subspaces? Is it possible to find these ``natural'' subspaces in a purely unsupervised way? Somewhat surprisingly, we can indeed achieve this and find interpretable subspaces by a seemingly unrelated training objective. Our method, neighbor distance minimization (NDM), learns non-basis-aligned subspaces in an unsupervised manner. Qualitative analysis shows subspaces are interpretable in many cases, and encoded information in obtained subspaces tends to share the same abstract concept across different inputs, making such subspaces similar to ``variables'' used by the model. We also conduct quantitative experiments using known circuits in GPT-2; results show a strong connection between subspaces and circuit variables. We also provide evidence showing scalability to 2B models by finding separate subspaces mediating context and parametric knowledge routing. Viewed more broadly, our findings offer a new perspective on understanding model internals and building circuits.

papers.title: Quantifying Structure in CLIP Embeddings: A Statistical Framework for Concept Interpretation
papers.research_question: How to quantify rotation-sensitive structures in CLIP embeddings and how to decompose embeddings into interpretable concepts with statistical guarantees?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a hypothesis testing framework to detect rotation-sensitive structure in CLIP embeddings and a post-hoc concept decomposition method that balances interpretability and reconstruction fidelity with statistical guarantees.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively quantifies rotation-sensitive structures in embeddings, and the decomposition method achieves both interpretability and high reconstruction fidelity, with applications to spurious correlation removal.
papers.key_findings:
The hypothesis test can distinguish between structured embeddings (e.g., ImageNet) and rotation-invariant noise (e.g., white noise).
The concept decomposition method yields interpretable concepts with high reconstruction fidelity, outperforming SpLiCE in reconstruction quality.
Removing spurious concepts identified by the method improves worst-group accuracy by 22.6% on Waterbirds and triples accuracy on iWildCam.
The method captures analogical relations between concepts, such as transforming 'single dog' to 'group of dogs' and applying to birds.
The method provides a flexible trade-off between sparsity and reconstruction fidelity by varying the number of concepts.
papers.limitation:
Assumes linearity in the embedding decomposition, which may overlook complex non-linear structures.
Interpretability of discovered concepts depends on the quality and scope of available text descriptions, which may introduce biases.
The hypothesis testing procedure does not explicitly handle structured, non-rotational noise patterns.
papers.abstract: Concept-based approaches, which aim to identify human-understandable concepts within a model's internal representations, are a promising method for interpreting embeddings from deep neural network models, such as CLIP. While these approaches help explain model behavior, current methods lack statistical rigor, making it challenging to validate identified concepts and compare different techniques. To address this challenge, we introduce a hypothesis testing framework that quantifies rotation-sensitive structures within the CLIP embedding space. Once such structures are identified, we propose a post-hoc concept decomposition method. Unlike existing approaches, it offers theoretical guarantees that discovered concepts represent robust, reproducible patterns (rather than method-specific artifacts) and outperforms other techniques in terms of reconstruction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that our concept-based decomposition algorithm effectively balances reconstruction accuracy with concept interpretability and helps mitigate spurious cues in data. Applied to a popular spurious correlation dataset, our method yields a 22.6% increase in worst-group accuracy after removing spurious background concepts.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: Understanding Empirical Unlearning with Combinatorial Interpretability
