SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Explaining Latent Representations with a Corpus of Examples
papers.research_question: How can we explain the latent representations of machine learning models? Specifically, which corpus examples explain the prediction for a test example, and what features of these corpus examples are relevant for the model to relate them to the test example?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SimplEx, a post-hoc method that explains latent representations by decomposing them as mixtures of examples from a user-chosen corpus, and introduces Integrated Jacobians to attribute feature-level contributions.
papers.conclusion: SimplEx provides robust and accurate example-based explanations of latent representations, empowering users to understand model predictions through meaningful corpus examples and feature attributions.
papers.key_findings:
SimplEx produces more accurate and robust approximations of latent representations compared to baselines like KNN and the representer theorem.
The Integrated Jacobian projections effectively identify which features of corpus examples are important for relating them to the test example.
SimplEx can detect out-of-distribution examples by analyzing corpus residuals.
The method allows users to choose any corpus, enabling personalized explanations.
Experiments on medical and image data show that SimplEx provides interpretable and useful explanations.
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models are complicated. Most of them rely on convoluted latent representations of their input to issue a prediction. To achieve greater transparency than a black-box that connects inputs to predictions, it is necessary to gain a deeper understanding of these latent representations. To that aim, we propose SimplEx: a user-centred method that provides example-based explanations with reference to a freely selected set of examples, called the corpus. SimplEx uses the corpus to improve the user's understanding of the latent space with post-hoc explanations answering two questions: (1) Which corpus examples explain the prediction issued for a given test example? (2) What features of these corpus examples are relevant for the model to relate them to the test example? SimplEx provides an answer by reconstructing the test latent representation as a mixture of corpus latent representations. Further, we propose a novel approach, the Integrated Jacobian, that allows SimplEx to make explicit the contribution of each corpus feature in the mixture. Through experiments on tasks ranging from mortality prediction to image classification, we demonstrate that these decompositions are robust and accurate. With illustrative use cases in medicine, we show that SimplEx empowers the user by highlighting relevant patterns in the corpus that explain model representations. Moreover, we demonstrate how the freedom in choosing the corpus allows the user to have personalized explanations in terms of examples that are meaningful for them.

papers.title: Measuring and Guiding Monosemanticity
papers.research_question: How can we systematically measure and improve the monosemanticity (single-concept encoding) of feature representations in large language models, specifically within Sparse Autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric for quantifying monosemanticity in latent representations, and proposes Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that uses latent conditioning during training to enforce isolated, monosemantic feature representations, improving interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: The introduced FMS metric and G-SAE method provide actionable guidelines for advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs by enabling reliable measurement and enforcement of monosemantic feature representations.
papers.key_findings:
G-SAE achieves significantly higher FMS scores than vanilla SAEs, indicating stronger feature monosemanticity, localization, and disentanglement.
G-SAE enables more effective and precise concept detection (e.g., toxicity, writing style, privacy attributes) compared to unsupervised SAEs.
Steering using G-SAE's decoder vectors allows for fine-grained control over model outputs (e.g., reducing toxicity, altering writing style) with less quality degradation than baseline methods.
The proposed FMS metric reveals critical shortcomings in the monosemanticity of features learned by standard, unsupervised SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The training of G-SAE requires labeled data for the target concepts, which may not always be available.
The method could be misused for adversarial steering to amplify undesirable model behaviors.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in leveraging mechanistic interpretability and controllability to better understand and influence the internal dynamics of large language models (LLMs). However, current methods face fundamental challenges in reliably localizing and manipulating feature representations. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a promising direction for feature extraction at scale, yet they, too, are limited by incomplete feature isolation and unreliable monosemanticity. To systematically quantify these limitations, we introduce Feature Monosemanticity Score (FMS), a novel metric to quantify feature monosemanticity in latent representation. Building on these insights, we propose Guided Sparse Autoencoders (G-SAE), a method that conditions latent representations on labeled concepts during training. We demonstrate that reliable localization and disentanglement of target concepts within the latent space improve interpretability, detection of behavior, and control. Specifically, our evaluations on toxicity detection, writing style identification, and privacy attribute recognition show that G-SAE not only enhances monosemanticity but also enables more effective and fine-grained steering with less quality degradation. Our findings provide actionable guidelines for measuring and advancing mechanistic interpretability and control of LLMs.

papers.title: I Predict Therefore I Am: Is Next Token Prediction Enough to Learn Human-Interpretable Concepts from Data?
papers.research_question: Is next-token prediction sufficient for large language models to learn human-interpretable concepts from data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes that LLM representations learned via next-token prediction are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent human-interpretable concepts, providing a theoretical foundation for the linear representation hypothesis and motivating a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: Next-token prediction enables LLMs to learn human-interpretable concepts, and the linear identifiability result offers a unified perspective on the linear representation hypothesis and a principled approach for evaluating concept disentanglement methods like sparse autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Under mild conditions, LLM representations are approximately a linear transformation of the log-posterior of latent concepts.
This linear property provides a unified explanation for empirical phenomena like concepts as directions and linear probing.
The linear property motivates a principled evaluation method for sparse autoencoders using linear probes.
Structured SAEs, which incorporate low-rank regularization, improve concept disentanglement compared to standard SAEs.
Empirical validation on simulation data and multiple LLM families (Pythia, Llama, DeepSeek) supports the theoretical results.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis relies on assumptions such as the diversity condition and approximate invertibility, which may not hold in all scenarios.
The evaluation of sparse autoencoders depends on the quality of linear probes, which may be noisy.
future_direction: Rethinking invertibility assumptions in causal representation learning.
Embedding causal reasoning in LLMs through linear unmixing.
papers.abstract: The remarkable achievements of large language models (LLMs) have led many to conclude that they exhibit a form of intelligence. This is as opposed to explanations of their capabilities based on their ability to perform relatively simple manipulations of vast volumes of data. To illuminate the distinction between these explanations, we introduce a novel generative model that generates tokens on the basis of human-interpretable concepts represented as latent discrete variables. Under mild conditions, even when the mapping from the latent space to the observed space is non-invertible, we establish an identifiability result, i.e., the representations learned by LLMs through next-token prediction can be approximately modeled as the logarithm of the posterior probabilities of these latent discrete concepts given input context, up to an invertible linear transformation. This theoretical finding not only provides evidence that LLMs capture underlying generative factors, but also provide a unified prospective for understanding of the linear representation hypothesis. Taking this a step further, our finding motivates a reliable evaluation of sparse autoencoders by treating the performance of supervised concept extractors as an upper bound. Pushing this idea even further, it inspires a structural variant that enforces dependence among latent concepts in addition to promoting sparsity. Empirically, we validate our theoretical results through evaluations on both simulation data and the Pythia, Llama, and DeepSeek model families, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our structured sparse autoencoder.

papers.title: The Confidence Manifold: Geometric Structure of Correctness Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of correctness representations in language models, and how can it be used for efficient detection of model errors?
papers.core_contribution: The discriminative signal for correctness in language models is low-dimensional (3-8 dimensions) and linearly separable; centroid distance in this subspace matches trained probe performance, enabling few-shot error detection.
papers.conclusion: The confidence manifold is simpler than expected, with a low-dimensional linear structure, enabling efficient geometric detection of model errors via centroid distance.
papers.key_findings:
The confidence signal occupies 3-8 dimensions, and adding more dimensions hurts performance.
The signal is linearly separable; no nonlinear classifier improves over linear probes.
Centroid distance in the low-dimensional subspace matches trained probe performance, enabling few-shot detection with minimal labels.
Internal probes achieve high AUC (0.80-0.97) while output-based methods like semantic entropy perform poorly (0.44-0.64).
Activation steering validates causality: the learned direction produces monotonic, 10.9 percentage point changes in error rates.
papers.limitation: The signal does not transfer well to tasks like HaluEval (summarization faithfulness), indicating specificity to factual QA.
papers.abstract: When a language model asserts that "the capital of Australia is Sydney," does it know this is wrong? We characterize the geometry of correctness representations across 9 models from 5 architecture families. The structure is simple: the discriminative signal occupies 3-8 dimensions, performance degrades with additional dimensions, and no nonlinear classifier improves over linear separation. Centroid distance in the low-dimensional subspace matches trained probe performance (0.90 AUC), enabling few-shot detection: on GPT-2, 25 labeled examples achieve 89% of full-data accuracy. We validate causally through activation steering: the learned direction produces 10.9 percentage point changes in error rates while random directions show no effect. Internal probes achieve 0.80-0.97 AUC; output-based methods (P(True), semantic entropy) achieve only 0.44-0.64 AUC. The correctness signal exists internally but is not expressed in outputs. That centroid distance matches probe performance indicates class separation is a mean shift, making detection geometric rather than learned.

papers.title: LUCID-SAE: Learning Unified Vision-Language Sparse Codes for Interpretable Concept Discovery
papers.research_question: Can we learn a single set of sparse codes whose units are directly comparable across vision and language spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LUCID, a unified vision-language sparse autoencoder that learns a shared latent dictionary for image patch and text token representations, enabling cross-modal feature alignment and automatic concept interpretation.
papers.conclusion: LUCID establishes aligned sparse dictionaries as a foundation for automatic interpretability at scale, providing a principled approach toward interpretable multimodal representations that support systematic cross-modal analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Shared-private decomposition improves both reconstruction fidelity and cross-modal predictability by shielding the shared space from modality-specific noise.
Optimal transport-based alignment enables precise patch-level grounding as measured by local spatial metrics.
Structured shared-code objectives mitigate clustering degeneracy while sharpening object-level grounding.
LUCID captures diverse concept categories spanning objects, scenes, actions, attributes, and spatial relationships, with learned representations generalizing to out-of-distribution data.
An automated neuron interpretation pipeline discovers coherent semantic clusters without manual annotation.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a natural path toward comparable explanations across different representation spaces. However, current SAEs are trained per modality, producing dictionaries whose features are not directly understandable and whose explanations do not transfer across domains. In this study, we introduce LUCID (Learning Unified vision-language sparse Codes for Interpretable concept Discovery), a unified vision-language sparse autoencoder that learns a shared latent dictionary for image patch and text token representations, while reserving private capacity for modality-specific details. We achieve feature alignment by coupling the shared codes with a learned optimal transport matching objective without the need of labeling. LUCID yields interpretable shared features that support patch-level grounding, establish cross-modal neuron correspondence, and enhance robustness against the concept clustering problem in similarity-based evaluation. Leveraging the alignment properties, we develop an automated dictionary interpretation pipeline based on term clustering without manual observations. Our analysis reveals that LUCID's shared features capture diverse semantic categories beyond objects, including actions, attributes, and abstract concepts, demonstrating a comprehensive approach to interpretable multimodal representations.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Encode Scientific Quality? An Empirical Study Using Monosemantic Features from Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode the concept of scientific quality using monosemantic features extracted from sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first systematic investigation into how LLMs encode scientific quality using monosemantic features from sparse autoencoders, identifying four key types of features related to research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode a rich and multidimensional representation of scientific quality through monosemantic features, capturing aspects like research methodologies, publication types, high-impact fields, and scientific jargon, providing insights into their internal mechanisms for research evaluation.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode features reflecting research methodologies, associating higher quality with rigorous methodological approaches.
Features related to publication type, such as survey papers and literature reviews, are associated with higher scholarly impact.
Features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies act as strong signals of perceived research importance.
Features corresponding to specific scientific jargons and academic language are identified, though their precise role is unclear.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of monosemantic features inherently involves a qualitative component, as semantic labels are assigned by human researchers and may introduce subjectivity.
This work focused exclusively on Gemma 2 models, limiting the generality of the results to other architectures.
The study classified publications into research quality quartiles rather than using regression to predict specific values.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other LLM architectures to assess the generality of the results.
Using regression to predict specific quality values instead of classification into quartiles.
Investigating how interpretable features can enhance LLM performance in tasks such as research evaluation, academic text generation, and hypothesis discovery.
papers.abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing use of generative AI, and large language models (LLMs) in particular, to support both the assessment and generation of scientific work. Although some studies have shown that LLMs can, to a certain extent, evaluate research according to perceived quality, our understanding of the internal mechanisms that enable this capability remains limited. This paper presents the first study that investigates how LLMs encode the concept of scientific quality through relevant monosemantic features extracted using sparse autoencoders. We derive such features under different experimental settings and assess their ability to serve as predictors across three tasks related to research quality: predicting citation count, journal SJR, and journal h-index. The results indicate that LLMs encode features associated with multiple dimensions of scientific quality. In particular, we identify four recurring types of features that capture key aspects of how research quality is represented: 1) features reflecting research methodologies; 2) features related to publication type, with literature reviews typically exhibiting higher impact; 3) features associated with high-impact research fields and technologies; and 4) features corresponding to specific scientific jargons. These findings represent an important step toward understanding how LLMs encapsulate concepts related to research quality.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How does attention in protein Transformer models capture structural and functional properties of proteins?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention in protein Transformer models captures the folding structure of proteins, targets binding sites, and focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and that such interpretability methods can potentially aid scientific discovery in biology.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in protein Transformers captures tertiary structure (contact maps).
Attention targets functional sites like binding sites and post-translational modifications.
Deeper layers focus on more complex properties (e.g., binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their attention patterns correlate with substitution matrices.
The findings are consistent across multiple Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT, XLNet) and datasets.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Leveraging attention to uncover novel relationships or more nuanced forms of existing measures such as contact maps.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations in other scientific domains.
papers.abstract:
Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for
protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations
present challenges in interpretability. In this work, we demonstrate a set of
methods for analyzing protein Transformer models through the lens of attention.
We show that attention: (1) captures the folding structure of proteins,
connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but
spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites,
a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more
complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We find this
behavior to be consistent across three Transformer architectures (BERT, ALBERT,
XLNet) and two distinct protein datasets. We also present a three-dimensional
visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Code
for visualization and analysis is available at
https://github.com/salesforce/provis.

papers.title: Sparsification and Reconstruction from the Perspective of Representation Geometry
papers.research_question: How does sparse encoding organize the representations of activation vectors from language models? What is the relationship between this organizational paradigm and feature disentanglement as well as reconstruction performance?
papers.core_contribution: This study explains the principles of sparsity from the perspective of representational geometry and demonstrates the impact of changes in representational structure on reconstruction performance, emphasizing the necessity of understanding representations and incorporating representational constraints.
papers.conclusion: The findings offer guidance for improving SAEs and developing novel tools for decomposing neural networks from the perspective of representation geometry, particularly emphasizing the necessity of understanding and incorporating representation geometry constraints.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit stratified manifolds where representations of the same concept are distributed across different manifolds.
Sparse encoding reduces feature overlap by merging similar semantic features within local representations and introducing more dimensionality, achieving feature disentanglement.
Increased separability between different local representations causally enhances reconstruction performance in SAEs.
The variability of the feature modal rank (r3) and AGD under noise validates the stratified structure of representations.
Global representations are compressed during sparse encoding, while local representations gain effective dimensionality and connected components.
papers.limitation:
Extraction of activations depends on prompts related to the concept, not guaranteeing all representations are captured.
Regularization in SAEs is not included as a controlled variable, and differences in representation structure caused by variations in regularization require further exploration.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a predominant tool in mechanistic interpretability, aiming to identify interpretable monosemantic features. However, how does sparse encoding organize the representations of activation vector from language models? What is the relationship between this organizational paradigm and feature disentanglement as well as reconstruction performance? To address these questions, we propose the SAEMA, which validates the stratified structure of the representation by observing the variability of the rank of the symmetric semipositive definite (SSPD) matrix corresponding to the modal tensor unfolded along the latent tensor with the level of noise added to the residual stream. To systematically investigate how sparse encoding alters representational structures, we define local and global representations, demonstrating that they amplify inter-feature distinctions by merging similar semantic features and introducing additional dimensionality. Furthermore, we intervene the global representation from an optimization perspective, proving a significant causal relationship between their separability and the reconstruction performance. This study explains the principles of sparsity from the perspective of representational geometry and demonstrates the impact of changes in representational structure on reconstruction performance. Particularly emphasizes the necessity of understanding representations and incorporating representational constraints, providing empirical references for developing new interpretable tools and improving SAEs. The code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/wenjie1835/SAERepGeo}{https://github.com/wenjie1835/SAERepGeo}.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Feature Integration Spaces: Joint Training Reveals Dual Encoding in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: Does neural network encode information in two complementary spaces: feature identity and feature integration?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides systematic evidence for dual encoding in neural representations, meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature integrations, and introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first systematic evidence for dual-encoding spaces in neural network representations and introduces an architectural solution that achieves substantial improvements across multiple validation metrics, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors over SAE-only baseline.
The architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization with low squared norm features specializing in integration pathways.
Integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce statistically significant nonlinear interaction effects on model outputs.
Nonlinear integration components achieve 16.5% standalone improvement using only 3% of parameters, demonstrating parameter efficiency.
Sequential SAE+NFM approach shows 23.4% error reduction and 29.8% reduction in pathological KL divergence errors.
papers.limitation:
Scale constraints represent one primary limitation of this work. Our experiments on a 3B parameter model with 50k SAE features provide proof-of-concept evidence, but scaling to industrial-scale models with millions of features is likely challenging.
Integration interpretability presents ongoing challenges. While we demonstrated functional effects, these features remain largely opaque to direct inspection.
Limitations of traditional feature discovery approaches, as maximum activation analysis on secondary features failed to yield interpretable patterns.
future_direction: Dynamic analysis of how integration patterns evolve during training
Cross-model validation
Cross-layer analysis
papers.abstract: Current sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches to neural network interpretability assume that activations can be decomposed through linear superposition into sparse, interpretable features. Despite high reconstruction fidelity, SAEs consistently fail to eliminate polysemanticity and exhibit pathological behavioral errors. We propose that neural networks encode information in two complementary spaces compressed into the same substrate: feature identity and feature integration. To test this dual encoding hypothesis, we develop sequential and joint-training architectures to capture identity and integration patterns simultaneously. Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors. This architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization: low squared norm features contributing to integration pathways and the rest contributing directly to the residual. Small nonlinear components (3% of parameters) achieve 16.5% standalone improvements, demonstrating parameter-efficient capture of computational relationships crucial for behavior. Additionally, intervention experiments using 2x2 factorial stimulus designs demonstrated that integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce systematic behavioral effects on model outputs, including significant statistical interaction effects across semantic dimensions. This work provides systematic evidence for (1) dual encoding in neural representations, (2) meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature interactions, and (3) introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.

papers.title: A simple probabilistic neural network for machine understanding
papers.research_question: What are the properties of learning machines with a fixed internal representation, derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, in unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM), a probabilistic neural network with a fixed internal representation derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, and shows that it has desirable properties like continuity, controllable compression, and ability to support functions beyond generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that learning machines with a fixed internal representation, such as the HFM, operate in a qualitatively different regime from traditional models like RBMs, with data-specific information stored in weights and potential for higher cognitive functions.
papers.key_findings:
The HFM is uniquely identified by the principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance when hidden units are binary.
The HFM exhibits a phase transition at a critical coupling parameter g, with a divergence in specific heat.
Training the HFM with an EM algorithm allows features to be learned sequentially, with low-order features remaining stable as new features are added.
The internal representation of the HFM is robust to changes in the coupling parameter and dataset size, and low-order features capture most of the relevant information.
The learning modality of HFM is qualitatively different from RBMs: in HFM, data-specific information is stored in the weights, while in RBMs it is transferred to the internal representation.
future_direction: Investigating whether a universal data-independent internal representation emerges spontaneously in deep layers of learning architectures.
Relating the findings to thermodynamic costs of learning.
Exploring the hypothesis that internal representations evolve with depth in hierarchical learning systems.
papers.abstract: We discuss probabilistic neural networks with a fixed internal representation as models for machine understanding. Here understanding is intended as mapping data to an already existing representation which encodes an {\em a priori} organisation of the feature space. We derive the internal representation by requiring that it satisfies the principles of maximal relevance and of maximal ignorance about how different features are combined. We show that, when hidden units are binary variables, these two principles identify a unique model -- the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) -- which is fully solvable and provides a natural interpretation in terms of features. We argue that learning machines with this architecture enjoy a number of interesting properties, like the continuity of the representation with respect to changes in parameters and data, the possibility to control the level of compression and the ability to support functions that go beyond generalisation. We explore the behaviour of the model with extensive numerical experiments and argue that models where the internal representation is fixed reproduce a learning modality which is qualitatively different from that of traditional models such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines.

papers.title: Mapping Clinical Doubt: Locating Linguistic Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: How are epistemic signals encoding linguistic uncertainty represented across the layers of LLMs, and are these representations stable across model variants?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layer-wise probing metric, and demonstrates that LLMs encode linguistic uncertainty progressively in deeper layers, with sensitivity increasing monotonically with depth.
papers.conclusion: Encoding of epistemic uncertainty is a distributed and emergent property in transformer architectures, peaking in final layers, and the MSU metric provides a targeted lens for interpretability and epistemic awareness.
papers.key_findings:
MSU scores increase monotonically with depth across all tested models, indicating greater sensitivity to epistemic uncertainty in later layers.
PCA reveals clustering and geometric inversion in deeper layers, suggesting semantic reorganization of uncertainty representations.
Later layers exhibit substantially higher sensitivity to epistemic modals, aligning with their role in encoding abstract semantics.
The pattern of late-emerging sensitivity is consistent across different model families and instruction-tuning variants.
Uncertainty is treated as a high-level semantic feature that is progressively amplified across the transformer stack.
papers.limitation: Findings are based on a limited set of instruction-tuned models, so their generality across architectures, sizes, and pretraining paradigms remains uncertain.
future_direction: Expand to diverse model types, including non-instruct, multilingual, and domain-specific models.
Localize uncertainty to specific neurons or attention heads.
Examine how internal uncertainty signals (e.g., logits, entropy) relate to output confidence and calibration.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, where sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty can influence diagnostic interpretation and decision-making. Yet little is known about where such epistemic cues are internally represented within these models. Distinct from uncertainty quantification, which measures output confidence, this work examines input-side representational sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty in medical text. We curate a contrastive dataset of clinical statements varying in epistemic modality (e.g., 'is consistent with' vs. 'may be consistent with') and propose Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layerwise probing metric that quantifies activation-level shifts induced by uncertainty cues. Our results show that LLMs exhibit structured, depth-dependent sensitivity to clinical uncertainty, suggesting that epistemic information is progressively encoded in deeper layers. These findings reveal how linguistic uncertainty is internally represented in LLMs, offering insight into their interpretability and epistemic reliability.

papers.title: The Mythos of Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the motivations for interpretability in machine learning, and what properties or techniques are thought to confer interpretability to models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a critical analysis of the concept of interpretability in machine learning, arguing that the term is ill-defined and encompasses diverse and sometimes conflicting motivations and notions, and that claims about interpretability must be qualified with specific definitions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the machine learning community must critically engage with the problem formulation of interpretability, and that researchers and practitioners share responsibility for ensuring machine learning aligns with societal desiderata.
papers.key_findings:
Linear models are not strictly more interpretable than deep neural networks; the validity of such a claim depends on the specific notion of interpretability being used (e.g., algorithmic transparency vs. decomposability).
Claims about interpretability must be qualified by specifying the definition of interpretability being employed, as the term refers to multiple distinct concepts.
In some cases, the desire for model transparency may conflict with broader objectives of AI, such as achieving higher predictive performance.
Post-hoc interpretations can potentially mislead, especially if they are optimized to produce plausible but unfaithful explanations.
The demand for interpretability often arises from a mismatch between formal machine learning objectives (e.g., test set performance) and real-world deployment costs or desiderata.
future_direction: Developing richer loss functions and performance metrics to mitigate the discrepancy between real-life and machine learning objectives.
Expanding the analysis of interpretability to other machine learning paradigms such as reinforcement learning.
Addressing challenges like fairness and contestability in the context of interpretability.
papers.abstract: In machine learning, the concept of interpretability is both important and slippery.

papers.title: How 'Neural' is a Neural Foundation Model?
papers.research_question: Do neural decoding and encoding manifolds reveal new insights into how foundation models represent temporal response patterns? Are their representations brain-like?
papers.core_contribution: The recurrent module of the neural foundation model shows brain-like representational properties, while the feedforward encoder and readout module have limitations; design changes are suggested for better biological alignment.
papers.conclusion: The FNN is only a partial digital twin of the mouse visual system; its recurrent module is most brain-like, but design improvements in early recurrence and readout constraints could enhance biological alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The recurrent module achieves the highest stimulus separability and closest alignment with biological visual cortex.
The feedforward encoder lacks biologically plausible temporal patterns and contains non-selective neurons.
The readout module uses numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms.
Decoding trajectories in the recurrent stage show tubular structure but fewer crossings than biological data, indicating less complex dynamics.
Encoding manifolds reveal that the FNN's neuronal organization, especially in the readout, is clustered by feature maps and differs from the continuous topology of biological cortex.
papers.limitation:
The FNN does not fully capture the complexity of neural dynamics, as evidenced by fewer crossings in decoding trajectories compared to biological data.
The readout module's highly clustered, feature-map-based organization is not brain-like.
future_direction: Introduce recurrence in early encoder stages.
Constraining features in the readout module to be more biologically plausible.
Investigate more complex temporal processing to better match biological dynamics.
papers.abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success in fitting biological visual systems; however, their black-box nature inherently limits their utility for understanding brain function. Here, we peek inside a SOTA foundation model of neural activity (Wang et al., 2025) as a physiologist might, characterizing each 'neuron' based on its temporal response properties to parametric stimuli. We analyze how different stimuli are represented in neural activity space by building decoding manifolds, and we analyze how different neurons are represented in stimulus-response space by building neural encoding manifolds. We find that the different processing stages of the model (i.e., the feedforward encoder, recurrent, and readout modules) each exhibit qualitatively different representational structures in these manifolds. The recurrent module shows a jump in capabilities over the encoder module by 'pushing apart' the representations of different temporal stimulus patterns. Our 'tubularity' metric quantifies this stimulus-dependent development of neural activity as biologically plausible. The readout module achieves high fidelity by using numerous specialized feature maps rather than biologically plausible mechanisms. Overall, this study provides a window into the inner workings of a prominent neural foundation model, gaining insights into the biological relevance of its internals through the novel analysis of its neurons' joint temporal response patterns. Our findings suggest design changes that could bring neural foundation models into closer alignment with biological systems: introducing recurrence in early encoder stages, and constraining features in the readout module.

papers.title: CytoSAE: Interpretable Cell Embeddings for Hematology
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be applied for interpretable morphological concept discovery in hematological imaging?
papers.core_contribution: CytoSAE is a sparse autoencoder that discovers interpretable morphological concepts in hematological images, generalizes across diverse and out-of-domain datasets, and enables explainable disease classification at patch, image, patient, and disease levels.
papers.conclusion: CytoSAE successfully learns interpretable morphological features across different hematological datasets, maintains generalizability to out-of-domain data, and enables multi-level analysis for interpretable disease classification.
papers.key_findings:
CytoSAE discovers morphologically relevant concepts that generalize across peripheral blood and bone marrow cytology datasets, validated by medical experts.
Patch-wise attribution allows sub-cellular level analysis of concepts, highlighting consistent morphological features across datasets.
Patient-level concept barcodes reveal disease-specific morphological features for AML subtypes, such as monocytic precursors for CBFB::MYH11 and granulated blasts for PML::RARA.
CytoSAE concepts achieve multi-class classification performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning methods while providing explainability.
Ablation studies show the number of discovered concepts is stable across expansion factors and hyperparameters, with optimal layers between 7–11 for concept balance.
papers.limitation: Manual expert validation was conducted only at the dataset level, not per patient, to avoid human selection bias in concept discovery.
future_direction: Explore patient-specific concept retrieval while minimizing subjectivity.
Incorporate semi-supervised learning techniques to refine the discovered features further.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) emerged as a promising tool for mechanistic interpretability of transformer-based foundation models. Very recently, SAEs were also adopted for the visual domain, enabling the discovery of visual concepts and their patch-wise attribution to tokens in the transformer model. While a growing number of foundation models emerged for medical imaging, tools for explaining their inferences are still lacking. In this work, we show the applicability of SAEs for hematology. We propose CytoSAE, a sparse autoencoder which is trained on over 40,000 peripheral blood single-cell images. CytoSAE generalizes to diverse and out-of-domain datasets, including bone marrow cytology, where it identifies morphologically relevant concepts which we validated with medical experts. Furthermore, we demonstrate scenarios in which CytoSAE can generate patient-specific and disease-specific concepts, enabling the detection of pathognomonic cells and localized cellular abnormalities at the patch level. We quantified the effect of concepts on a patient-level AML subtype classification task and show that CytoSAE concepts reach performance comparable to the state-of-the-art, while offering explainability on the sub-cellular level. Source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/dynamical-inference/cytosae.

papers.title: Exploiting Latent Linearity in LLMs Improves Explainable Molecular Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can LLM-derived molecular representations be linearly decomposed into chemically meaningful concepts (functional groups), and how can this latent linearity be exploited for explainable molecular property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MoleX, a framework that decomposes LLM latent representations into a concept-aligned space of functional groups and shows that a sparse linear mapping onto these chemical concepts improves both predictive accuracy and explainability for molecular property prediction.
papers.conclusion: Exploiting latent linearity in LLM representations provides a principled basis for effective and explainable molecular representation learning, improving accuracy, explainability, and efficiency in molecular property prediction.
papers.key_findings:
LLM-derived molecular representations exhibit latent linearity that can be expressed as a weighted combination of chemically meaningful functional group concepts.
MoleX outperforms existing GNN, LLM, and explainable machine learning baselines in predictive accuracy and explanation faithfulness on benchmark molecular property prediction tasks.
A residual calibration strategy corrects errors from the base linear predictor, further improving accuracy and explanation alignment with ground-truth substructures.
MoleX achieves significant computational efficiency, with CPU inference over 300x faster than LLMs and using 100,000 fewer parameters.
The linear predictor's performance scales with model size, training precision, and dataset size, but task-adapted training is crucial for converting capacity into performance gains.
papers.limitation: The linear predictor may underfit complex molecular patterns in some cases, as there is a trade-off between model complexity and performance.
future_direction: Examine the complexity–performance trade-off in LLM-based molecular representation learning to identify optimal balances between model complexity and downstream performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated broad utility across molecular domains, spanning drug discovery and materials design. Analyzing LLMs' latent representations is crucial for elucidating their underlying mechanisms, improving explainability, and ultimately advancing downstream performance. We propose MoleX, a simple yet effective framework that decomposes molecular embeddings within LLM representations into a concept-aligned space for explainable molecular representation learning. We further show that these high-dimensional embeddings admit a linear mapping onto chemically consistent concepts. Our analysis suggests that the uncovered linearity aligns with established chemical principles, indicating a mechanistically explainable latent structure in LLM representations for scientific applications. When applied to downstream tasks, this latent linearity improves both predictive and explanatory performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MoleX outperforms existing approaches in accuracy, explainability, and efficiency, achieving CPU inference on large-scale datasets 300 times faster with 100,000 fewer parameters than LLMs.

papers.title: Invertible Neural Networks for Understanding Semantics of Invariances of CNN Representations
papers.research_question: How can we understand the semantic concepts and invariances learned by deep neural networks (specifically CNNs) by recovering the invariances and translating the representations into an interpretable form without modifying the original model?
papers.core_contribution: An invertible neural network (INN) approach that recovers the invariances a deep model has learned and bijectively translates the model representation and its invariances into a semantically accessible encoding without compromising the original model's performance.
papers.conclusion: The invertible approach provides a powerful, post-hoc diagnostic pipeline for explaining deep representations by recovering invariances and enabling semantic interpretation without retraining the model.
papers.key_findings:
The method visualizes representations and their invariances without artifacts, outperforming existing network inversion methods.
Analysis of FaceNet shows that invariances (e.g., to pose) increase with layer depth, while some features (e.g., glasses) remain identity-relevant across layers.
The approach can quantify how much of a semantic concept (e.g., texture vs. shape) is captured by a model's representation, revealing biases like texture bias in ImageNet-trained CNNs.
Semantic modifications in the interpretable space correctly alter the original representation and can be visualized, enabling diagnostic probing of model sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Abstract To tackle increasingly complex tasks, it has become an essential ability of neural networks to learn abstract representations. These task-specific representations and, particularly, the invariances they capture turn neural networks into black-box models that lack interpretability. To open such a black box, it is, therefore, crucial to uncover the different semantic concepts a model has learned as well as those that it has learned to be invariant to. We present an approach based on invertible neural networks (INNs) that (i) recovers the task-specific, learned invariances by disentangling the remaining factor of variation in the data and that (ii) invertibly transforms these recovered invariances combined with the model representation into an equally expressive one with accessible semantic concepts. As a consequence, neural network representations become understandable by providing the means to (i) expose their semantic meaning, (ii) semantically modify a representation, and (iii) visualize individual learned semantic concepts and invariances. Our invertible approach significantly extends the abilities to understand black-box models by enabling post hoc interpretations of state-of-the-art networks without compromising their performance. Our implementation is available at https://compvis.github.io/invariances/ .

papers.title: A Monosemantic Attribution Framework for Stable Interpretability in Clinical Neuroscience Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we produce stable, clinically meaningful explanations from large language models by integrating attributional and mechanistic interpretability to address polysemanticity and inter-method variability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified interpretability framework that integrates attributional and mechanistic perspectives through monosemantic feature extraction, using sparse autoencoders to transform polysemantic activations and an explanation optimizer (TEO) to produce stable and clinically meaningful explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed monosemantic attribution framework advances the safe and trustworthy application of LLMs in cognitive health and neurodegenerative disease by providing stable and clinically meaningful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The SAE layer improves attribution stability (lower RIS/ROS) and clinical meaningfulness.
TEO with SAE (TEO-SAE) achieves the most stable attributions across in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets.
The UMAP linear constraint helps linearize the attribution space and yields robust scores.
The framework provides clinically interpretable attribution maps highlighting relevant biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis.
SAE-guided attribution yields more reliable explanations than traditional attribution methods.
papers.abstract: Interpretability remains a key challenge for deploying large language models (LLMs) in clinical settings such as Alzheimer's disease progression diagnosis, where early and trustworthy predictions are essential. Existing attribution methods exhibit high inter-method variability and unstable explanations due to the polysemantic nature of LLM representations, while mechanistic interpretability approaches lack direct alignment with model inputs and outputs and do not provide explicit importance scores. We introduce a unified interpretability framework that integrates attributional and mechanistic perspectives through monosemantic feature extraction. By constructing a monosemantic embedding space at the level of an LLM layer and optimizing the framework to explicitly reduce inter-method variability, our approach produces stable input-level importance scores and highlights salient features via a decompressed representation of the layer of interest, advancing the safe and trustworthy application of LLMs in cognitive health and neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: Sum-of-Parts: Self-Attributing Neural Networks with End-to-End Learning of Feature Groups
papers.research_question: How can we design self-attributing neural networks that achieve high performance while maintaining interpretability? The paper proposes a group-based SANN framework with learnable feature groups.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Sum-of-Parts (SOP), a framework that transforms any differentiable model into a group-based self-attributing neural network with end-to-end learnable feature groups, achieving state-of-the-art performance and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SOP is a framework that transforms any model into a group-based self-attributing neural network, achieving state-of-the-art performance and interpretability, with applications in model debugging and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Per-feature SANNs have a lower bound on error that grows with feature dimension, while group-based SANNs can achieve zero error.
SOP achieves state-of-the-art performance among SANNs on vision and language tasks.
SOP's learned groups are interpretable and faithful according to quantitative and semantic metrics.
SOP explanations are useful for model debugging, e.g., identifying reliance on background vs. objects.
SOP enables scientific discovery in cosmology, revealing insights about galaxy formation.
papers.limitation:
SOP requires multiple forward passes (20 in our experiments) which can be computationally expensive.
The group generator and selector are trained end-to-end, which may require careful hyperparameter tuning.
The interpretability of groups depends on the backbone model and the task.
future_direction: Scaling SOP to larger models and datasets.
Exploring different group generation mechanisms.
Applying SOP to other domains such as healthcare and finance.
papers.abstract: Self-attributing neural networks (SANNs) present a potential path towards interpretable models for high-dimensional problems, but often face significant trade-offs in performance. In this work, we formally prove a lower bound on errors of per-feature SANNs, whereas group-based SANNs can achieve zero error and thus high performance. Motivated by these insights, we propose Sum-of-Parts (SOP), a framework that transforms any differentiable model into a group-based SANN, where feature groups are learned end-to-end without group supervision. SOP achieves state-of-the-art performance for SANNs on vision and language tasks, and we validate that the groups are interpretable on a range of quantitative and semantic metrics. We further validate the utility of SOP explanations in model debugging and cosmological scientific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/BrachioLab/sop

papers.title: A Survey of the Interpretability Aspect of Deep Learning Models
papers.research_question: This paper surveys the interpretability of deep learning models, classifying previous work and identifying gaps for future improvement.
papers.core_contribution: This survey paper provides a classification of interpretability research in deep learning and identifies gaps for future work, aiming to establish a comprehensive framework for interpretable deep learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper surveys interpretability in deep learning, highlighting the need for a comprehensive framework and terminology to guide future research and application.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability is a multi-dimensional concept involving simulatability, decomposability, and computational accountability.
Post-hoc interpretations can be textual, visual, local, or by instance, as categorized in the literature.
There is a trade-off between model interpretability and predictive accuracy, with simpler models often being more interpretable but less accurate.
Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL) offers a potential unified framework for modeling, reasoning, and interpretability.
Challenges remain in ensuring fairness, accountability, and the distinction between explainability and interpretability in deployed models.
papers.limitation: There is a trade-off between interpretability and accuracy in models, which is a challenge for deploying complex models in critical applications.
future_direction: Developing a comprehensive paradigm and terminology for interpretable deep learning.
Addressing challenges in fairness and accountability in interpretable models.
Exploring Bayesian deep learning as a unified framework for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have attained near-human degree of quality in images, textual, audio, and video recording categorization and predictions tasks. The networks, on the other hand, are still typically thought of as black-box functional probabilistic models that transfer an input data to a trained classifier. Integrating these systems into mission-critical activities like clinical diagnosis, scheduling, and management is the next stage in this human-machine evolutionary change, and it necessitates a degree of confidence in the technology output. Statistical measures are often employed to estimate an output's volatility. The idea of trust, on the other hand, is dependent on a human's sight into a machine's inner workings. To put it another way, the neural networks must justify its outputs in a way that is intelligible to humans, leading to new insights into its internal workings. "Interpretable deep networks" is the name we give to such networks. The concept of interpretability is not one-dimensional. Indeed, the variability of an interpretation owing to varying degrees of human comprehension necessitates the existence of a plethora of characteristics that together define interpretability. Furthermore, the model's interpretations may be expressed in terms of low-level network variables or input properties. We describe several of the variables that are helpful for model interpretability in this study, as well as previous work on those dimensions. We do a gap analysis to determine what remains to be improved to increase models interpretability as step of the procedure.

papers.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
papers.research_question: How can we engineer monosemanticity in toy models? Specifically, can models be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to different minima, and how do bias and number of neurons affect monosemanticity?
papers.core_contribution: Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to minima with moderate negative biases, and increasing the number of neurons per layer increases monosemanticity at the cost of compute.
papers.conclusion: Engineering monosemanticity in toy models is possible via negative biases and wider layers, pointing to future work on robust engineering and understanding polysemantic models.
papers.key_findings:
Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by changing which local minimum training finds.
More monosemantic minima have moderate negative biases, enabling engineering of highly monosemantic models via negative bias initialization and weight decay.
Providing more neurons per layer makes models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost.
In engineered monosemantic models, monosemantic neurons implement a simple algorithm balancing feature recovery against interference, and polysemantic neurons implement a low-rank linear map adjusting confidence.
The conclusions hold for various activation functions and feature frequency distributions.
papers.limitation:
The engineering approach is fragile because it depends on setting a bias weight decay rate that must be slow relative to the rate at which the model learns the task.
Naive introduction of sparsity in model weights results in significant reductions in task performance.
future_direction: Make the bias engineering more robust by tailoring bias decay per neuron or tying it to weight changes, or using regularizers.
Understand the algorithm implemented by highly polysemantic models.
Find ways to reduce compute cost of wider layers without excessive performance degradation.
papers.abstract: In some neural networks, individual neurons correspond to natural ``features'' in the input. Such \emph{monosemantic} neurons are of great help in interpretability studies, as they can be cleanly understood. In this work we report preliminary attempts to engineer monosemanticity in toy models. We find that models can be made more monosemantic without increasing the loss by just changing which local minimum the training process finds. More monosemantic loss minima have moderate negative biases, and we are able to use this fact to engineer highly monosemantic models. We are able to mechanistically interpret these models, including the residual polysemantic neurons, and uncover a simple yet surprising algorithm. Finally, we find that providing models with more neurons per layer makes the models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost. These findings point to a number of new questions and avenues for engineering monosemanticity, which we intend to study these in future work.

papers.title: Do Llamas understand the periodic table?
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) represent the periodic table of elements, and what is the geometric structure of their hidden states?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally develop structured geometric representations (a 3D spiral) of the periodic table in their hidden states, with knowledge encoded as continuous manifolds in middle layers that sharpen into categorical distinctions in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent symbolic scientific knowledge as coherent, geometry-aware manifolds that reflect the natural order of the physical world, which can inform interpretability and trust in LLMs for scientific applications.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure in LLM hidden states aligns with the conceptual organization of the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous, overlapping attribute subspaces, while deeper layers sharpen decision boundaries and integrate linguistic context.
Linguistic structure increasingly shapes factual representations in later layers.
Strong linear associations between related attributes in middle layers enable indirect recall.
Regression probing shows continuous numerical features are effectively represented in intermediate layers, while classification probing shows later layers are better for fine-grained categorical decisions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to chemical elements in the periodic table; future studies could expand to other chemical structures and properties.
The hypothesis-driven validation of geometric structures may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Expand to other chemical structures and properties.
Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge.
papers.abstract: We observe a 3D spiral structure in the hidden states of LLMs that aligns with the conceptual structure of the periodic table.

papers.title: Encoding and Understanding Astrophysical Information in Large Language Model-Generated Summaries
papers.research_question: To what extent does prompt engineering affect the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities, and how is physics information encoded in text summaries?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can encode physical information from astrophysical text, with structured prompting improving alignment between embeddings and physical quantities, and sparse autoencoders reveal the semantic concepts driving this encoding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can capture, learn, and represent physics concepts in textual data, and prompt engineering enhances the correlation between text embeddings and physical quantities. Sparse autoencoders provide insight into the semantic concepts underlying this encoding.
papers.key_findings:
Structured prompts significantly improve the clustering purity of LLM embeddings with respect to physical quantities, with improvements up to 57.5% for variability index.
Sparse autoencoders extract interpretable features from text embeddings that correlate with specific astrophysical properties, such as non-thermal characteristics linked to power-law gamma values.
LLMs infer physical parameters from text descriptions even when numerical values are not explicitly stated, demonstrating an understanding of astrophysical concepts.
Concepts like 'eclipsing binaries' and 'galaxy cluster thermal dynamics' are encoded in the embeddings and associated with physical measurements.
The method allows for visual and quantitative analysis of how physics is encoded in language through t-SNE clustering and SAE feature activation.
future_direction: Expanding the dataset to include more sources
Optimizing prompting with different models
Creating an interface for astronomer validation of possibly anomalous objects
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated the ability to generalize well at many levels across domains, modalities, and even shown in-context learning capabilities. This enables research questions regarding how they can be used to encode physical information that is usually only available from scientific measurements, and loosely encoded in textual descriptions. Using astrophysics as a test bed, we investigate if LLM embeddings can codify physical summary statistics that are obtained from scientific measurements through two main questions: 1) Does prompting play a role on how those quantities are codified by the LLM? and 2) What aspects of language are most important in encoding the physics represented by the measurement? We investigate this using sparse autoencoders that extract interpretable features from the text.

papers.title: Embracing Foundation Models for Advancing Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Machine learning foundation models, particularly large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4o, have revolutionized traditional applications in computer vision and natural language processing, marking a significant shift in recent years. Building on these advancements, recent efforts have explored the potential of foundation models in hypothesis generation, highlighting their possibility in aiding human researchers in scientific discovery. In this paper, we envision a future where academia increasingly integrates foundation models to accelerate and enhance the process of scientific discovery. Motivated by potential application scenarios of foundation models in scientific research, our vision is anchored in a central question: How can we accelerate scientific discovery with the aid of foundation models? To address this overarching question, we raise two key challenges that need to be addressed: (1) how to effectively harness the parametric knowledge embedded in foundation models to propel scientific discovery? and (2) how to develop rigorous yet scalable methods to evaluate the effectiveness of foundation models in supporting scientific research? To tackle these two challenges, we propose our approaches, termed knowledge-grounded Chain-of-Idea (KG-CoI) hypothesis generation and IdeaBench - Benchmarking LLM hypothesis generators in a customizable manner. Through addressing these challenges, we outline our vision in hope to inspire new ideas and innovations in harnessing foundation models for advancing scientific discovery, paving the way for a new era of research collaboration between humans and artificial intelligence.

papers.title: A Perspective on Foundation Models in Chemistry
papers.abstract: Foundation models are an emerging paradigm in artificial intelligence (AI), with successful examples like ChatGPT transforming daily workflows. Generally, foundation models are large-scale, pretrained models capable of adapting to various downstream tasks by leveraging extensive data and model scaling. Their success has inspired researchers to develop foundation models for a wide range of chemical challenges, from materials discovery to understanding structure-property relationships, areas where conventional machine learning (ML) models often face limitations. In addition, foundation models hold promise for addressing persistent ML challenges in chemistry, such as data scarcity and poor generalization. In this perspective, we review recent progress in the development of foundation models in chemistry across applications of varying scope. We also discuss emerging trends and provide an outlook on promising approaches for advancing foundation models in chemistry.

papers.title: An open-source family of large encoder-decoder foundation models for chemistry
papers.abstract: The use of foundation models has extended from natural language processing to molecular modeling. In this context, large-scale pre-training strategies have been applied to chemical language models to enable representation learning across diverse tasks. Here we introduce a family of encoder-decoder chemical foundation models pre-trained on a curated dataset of 91 million molecular sequences from PubChem. These models support a range of applications, including property estimation and reaction outcome prediction. We evaluate two model variants across several benchmark datasets and show that they match or exceed existing approaches. We also assess the structure of the learned representations and find that the embedding space supports few-shot learning and separates molecules based on chemically relevant features. This structure appears to result from the decoder-based reconstruction objective used during pre-training. These findings suggest that the proposed models can serve as general-purpose tools for molecular analysis and reasoning with minimal supervision.

papers.title: On Foundation Models for Temporal Point Processes to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Many scientific fields, from medicine to seismology, rely on analyzing sequences of events over time to understand complex systems. Traditionally, machine learning models must be built and trained from scratch for each new dataset, which is a slow and costly process. We introduce a new approach: a single, powerful model that learns the underlying patterns of event data in context. We trained this "foundation model" on millions of simulated event sequences, teaching it a general-purpose understanding of how events can unfold. As a result, our model can analyze new scientific data instantly, without retraining, simply by looking at a few examples from the dataset. It can also be quickly fine-tuned for even higher accuracy. This approach makes sophisticated event analysis more accessible and accelerates the pace of scientific discovery.
