This motivates a principled framework for concept extraction, namely Concept Component Analysis (ConCA), which aims to recover the log-posterior of each concept from LLM representations through a {unsupervised} linear unmixing process. We explore a specific variant, termed sparse ConCA, which leverages a sparsity prior to address the inherent ill-posedness of the unmixing problem. We implement 12 sparse ConCA variants and demonstrate their ability to extract meaningful concepts across multiple LLMs, offering theory-backed advantages over SAEs.

papers.title: Using Causal Analysis for Conceptual Deep Learning Explanation
papers.research_question: How to provide clinically relevant explanations for deep learning models in healthcare by associating hidden units with concepts and using causal analysis to ensure influence.
papers.core_contribution: A framework for explaining black-box models using clinically relevant concepts and causal mediation analysis to ensure concepts causally influence the model's decisions.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework provides global explanations for black-box models in terms of clinically relevant concepts that are causally influencing the model's decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept classifiers using sparse logistic regression achieve high recall, indicating effective association of hidden units with concepts.
Hidden units act as visual concept detectors, localizing radiographic features without explicit concept supervision during training.
Causal mediation analysis via counterfactual interventions ranks concepts based on indirect effect, with top-ranked concepts being clinically consistent.
The indirect effect is highest in middle layers (dense-block 3), showing their role in mediating decisions.
A decision tree surrogate function provides interpretable global explanations using the top-ranked concepts.
future_direction: Extend concept definition to include a broader set of clinical metrics.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: VISTA: A Panoramic View of Neural Representations
papers.research_question: How to visually explore and interpret neural network representations by mapping them into semantic 2D spaces to uncover patterns and relationships?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VISTA, a visualization pipeline that uses clustering and text-to-image models to create semantic 2D maps of neural representations, enabling interactive exploration and interpretation.
papers.conclusion: VISTA provides a visual, interactive method for interpreting neural representations that complements automated techniques and offers deeper insights into model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
VISTA confirms automated interpretations from LLM-based methods, validating its basic functionality.
VISTA discovers additional patterns not captured by automated methods, such as secondary triggers for certain latents.
VISTA reveals unexpected associations in latents, highlighting potential limitations in current automated techniques.
papers.limitation: Potential domain skew between datasets or limitations in automated techniques may affect interpretation, as seen in case study 3.
future_direction: Applying VISTA to a broader range of neural representations and integrating it with existing interpretability pipelines.
papers.abstract: We present VISTA (Visualization of Internal States and Their Associations), a novel pipeline for visually exploring and interpreting neural network representations. VISTA addresses the challenge of analyzing vast multidimensional spaces in modern machine learning models by mapping representations into a semantic 2D space. The resulting collages visually reveal patterns and relationships within internal representations. We demonstrate VISTA's utility by applying it to sparse autoencoder latents uncovering new properties and interpretations. We review the VISTA methodology, present findings from our case study ( https://got.drib.net/latents/ ), and discuss implications for neural network interpretability across various domains of machine learning.

papers.title: Transformer Key-Value Memories Are Nearly as Interpretable as Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: To what extent does a proxy-based, artificial decomposition of neuron activations (e.g., via sparse autoencoders) empirically benefit model interpretation compared to the organic features already represented within the original model's feed-forward layers?
papers.core_contribution: Features from feed-forward key-value memories (FF-KV) are nearly as interpretable as those from sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and in some aspects (e.g., absorption, explained variance) even outperform SAEs, suggesting that FF-KV features serve as a strong baseline for interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: Proxy-based methods such as SAEs offer very limited empirical advantage over direct analysis of feed-forward layers, and FF-KV features should be included as a strong baseline in interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FF-KV features achieve comparable interpretability to SAE features across multiple automatic evaluation metrics from SAEBENCH.
FF-KV features sometimes outperform SAEs, e.g., in absorption (less redundancy) and explained variance (perfect by definition).
Human evaluation shows conceptual features can be found with almost equal ease from both FF-KV and SAEs.
Features discovered by proxy methods (e.g., Transcoders) often do not align with features in the original FF module, suggesting potential hallucination.
Increasing sparsity in FF-KV (via TopK) does not consistently improve interpretability across metrics.
papers.limitation:
SCR and TPP scores are highly unstable and should be treated as supplementary results.
The theoretical advantage of SAEs is not observed empirically through the current evaluation scheme.
future_direction: Further research on the faithfulness of learned features from proxy modules, with FF-KV features as grounding points.
Inclusion of FF-KV features as a baseline when assessing feature-discovery methods in interpretability.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability work on large language models (LLMs) has been increasingly dominated by a feature-discovery approach with the help of proxy modules. Then, the quality of features learned by, e.g., sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), is evaluated. This paradigm naturally raises a critical question: do such learned features have better properties than those already represented within the original model parameters, and unfortunately, only a few studies have made such comparisons systematically so far. In this work, we revisit the interpretability of feature vectors stored in feed-forward (FF) layers, given the perspective of FF as key-value memories, with modern interpretability benchmarks. Our extensive evaluation revealed that SAE and FFs exhibits a similar range of interpretability, although SAEs displayed an observable but minimal improvement in some aspects. Furthermore, in certain aspects, surprisingly, even vanilla FFs yielded better interpretability than the SAEs, and features discovered in SAEs and FFs diverged. These bring questions about the advantage of SAEs from both perspectives of feature quality and faithfulness, compared to directly interpreting FF feature vectors, and FF key-value parameters serve as a strong baseline in modern interpretability research.

papers.title: Predictive learning as a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations
papers.research_question: Does learning to predict future observations cause neural networks to extract low-dimensional latent structure from their sensory inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Predictive learning in neural networks leads to the emergence of low-dimensional internal representations that linearly encode the latent variables of the environment, a process that can be quantified using novel metrics like latent signal transfer and dimensionality gain.
papers.conclusion: Predictive learning is a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations from high-dimensional sensory inputs, which can be characterized by the introduced metrics and analytical tools.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive learning causes neural networks to form low-dimensional representations that map the latent structure of the sensory environment.
Latent space signal transfer occurs during learning, where latent variables become increasingly linearly decodable from the top principal components of the neural representation.
Dimensionality gain (the ratio of linear to nonlinear dimensionality) increases during predictive learning, indicating the extraction of a low-dimensional manifold from high-dimensional observations.
Predictive learning leads to the emergence of neurons with localized activations on the manifold (manifold cells).
Representations formed by predictive learning are more structured and better reflect the latent space than those formed by autoencoding (non-predictive learning).
future_direction: Further testing of the predictive learning framework in neural data.
Application of the framework to additional tasks beyond spatial exploration and arm-reaching.
Investigation of predictive learning as a general principle for representation formation in both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have recently achieved many successes in solving sequential processing and planning tasks. Their success is often ascribed to the emergence of the task's low-dimensional latent structure in the network activity - i.e., in the learned neural representations. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that a means for generating representations with easily accessed low-dimensional latent structure, possibly reflecting an underlying semantic organization, is through learning to predict observations about the world. Specifically, we ask whether and when network mechanisms for sensory prediction coincide with those for extracting the underlying latent variables. Using a recurrent neural network model trained to predict a sequence of observations we show that network dynamics exhibit low-dimensional but nonlinearly transformed representations of sensory inputs that map the latent structure of the sensory environment. We quantify these results using nonlinear measures of intrinsic dimensionality and linear decodability of latent variables, and provide mathematical arguments for why such useful predictive representations emerge. We focus throughout on how our results can aid the analysis and interpretation of experimental data.

papers.title: Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models
papers.research_question: Can language models internally distinguish between testing and deployment phases (evaluation awareness), and how can this capability be probed and steered?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that evaluation awareness is linearly represented in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and can be extracted using linear probes, and that steering with evaluation-awareness-relevant SAE features can partially uncover sandbagging behavior.
papers.conclusion: Modern language models develop internal representations that distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts; current evaluation scenarios may be readily identifiable as artificial, highlighting the need for more realistic evaluation frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes trained on model activations can detect evaluation contexts with high AUROC scores (up to 0.829).
The probes generalize across different evaluation and deployment prompt datasets.
Current safety evaluation prompts (e.g., for deception) are often classified as test-like, suggesting models may recognize them as artificial evaluations.
Steering with SAE features related to evaluation awareness can partially recover sandbagged capabilities on the WMDP benchmark, but linear probe steering had minimal impact.
Evaluation awareness representations are more distinctly encoded in earlier model layers (e.g., layers 23-24).
papers.limitation:
The evaluation awareness observed in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct may be less pronounced than in frontier models, raising concerns about generalizability.
Linear probes may not capture the full complexity of evaluation awareness, which may not be strictly one-dimensionally linear.
The experimental setup is a significant simplification compared to real-world scenarios of concern (e.g., extended agentic backdoor honeypots).
Steering attempts using linear probes and SAE features showed limited success in modifying sandbagging behavior.
future_direction: Comprehensive red-teaming with alternative probe training methods (e.g., logistic regression, PCA, non-linear probes).
Leveraging probes to enhance the realism of scheming honeypots via automated prompt authenticity enhancement.
Integrating probe-based detection into control protocols as a low-latency whitebox monitoring system.
papers.abstract: Language models can distinguish between testing and deployment phases -- a capability known as evaluation awareness. This has significant safety and policy implications, potentially undermining the reliability of evaluations that are central to AI governance frameworks and voluntary industry commitments. In this paper, we study evaluation awareness in Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. We show that linear probes can separate real-world evaluation and deployment prompts, suggesting that current models internally represent this distinction. We also find that current safety evaluations are correctly classified by the probes, suggesting that they already appear artificial or inauthentic to models. Our findings underscore the importance of ensuring trustworthy evaluations and understanding deceptive capabilities. More broadly, our work showcases how model internals may be leveraged to support blackbox methods in safety audits, especially for future models more competent at evaluation awareness and deception.

papers.title: Human-interpretable model explainability on high-dimensional data
papers.research_question: How to provide human-interpretable model explanations on high-dimensional data by using semantic latent features and adapting the Shapley framework.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for model explainability on high-dimensional data that encodes raw inputs into semantic latent features and applies Shapley explainability to these features, providing interpretable, theoretically-controlled explanations.
papers.conclusion: The framework offers a principled, flexible way to achieve human-interpretable explainability on complex models and is hoped to be widely applicable.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarially robust classifiers are less sensitive to high-frequency information compared to non-robust models.
Texture classification models depend on high-frequency periodic patterns in images.
Disentangled latent representations can correctly attribute model decisions to known factors of variation (e.g., scale and position in dSprites).
In CelebA, a model predicting attractiveness shows bias towards gender and age, as revealed by semantic explanations.
The framework provides interpretable explanations that are not possible with pixel-based methods.
papers.limitation: The quality of explanations depends on the semantic representation; if the representation is not well-disentangled, explanations may be corrupted.
papers.abstract: The importance of explainability in machine learning continues to grow, as both neural-network architectures and the data they model become increasingly complex. Unique challenges arise when a model's input features become high dimensional: on one hand, principled model-agnostic approaches to explainability become too computationally expensive; on the other, more efficient explainability algorithms lack natural interpretations for general users. In this work, we introduce a framework for human-interpretable explainability on high-dimensional data, consisting of two modules. First, we apply a semantically meaningful latent representation, both to reduce the raw dimensionality of the data, and to ensure its human interpretability. These latent features can be learnt, e.g. explicitly as disentangled representations or implicitly through image-to-image translation, or they can be based on any computable quantities the user chooses. Second, we adapt the Shapley paradigm for model-agnostic explainability to operate on these latent features. This leads to interpretable model explanations that are both theoretically controlled and computationally tractable. We benchmark our approach on synthetic data and demonstrate its effectiveness on several image-classification tasks.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can find a canonical set of units of analysis (unique, complete, and atomic features) in language models.
papers.core_contribution: SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis because smaller SAEs are incomplete (missing information) and larger SAEs learn composed, non-atomic features. The choice of SAE dictionary size should be pragmatic.
papers.conclusion: Alternative methods are required for identifying canonical units of analysis, and SAE practitioners should adopt a pragmatic approach to choosing dictionary size for interpretability tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE stitching reveals that larger SAEs contain novel latents that improve reconstruction when added to smaller SAEs, indicating smaller SAEs are incomplete.
SAE stitching shows that larger SAEs also contain reconstruction latents similar to those in smaller SAEs, but sometimes composed of multiple smaller latents.
Meta-SAEs can decompose larger SAE latents into interpretable meta-latents, demonstrating that larger SAE latents are not atomic.
Meta-latents are similar to latents found in smaller SAEs, suggesting larger SAE latents are compositions of smaller SAE latents.
The sparsity penalty in SAEs incentivizes the learning of composed features in larger dictionaries, rather than atomic features.
papers.limitation:
The study only examines two language models (GPT-2 Small and Gemma 2 2B) and does not include very large SAEs.
Associating SAE latents with interpretable concepts remains an open problem, and the methods do not identify canonical units nor the optimal dictionary size.
future_direction: Pursue different approaches for identifying canonical units of analysis.
Pragmatically choose SAE dictionary size based on the specific interpretability task.
papers.abstract: A common goal of mechanistic interpretability is to decompose the activations of neural networks into features: interpretable properties of the input computed by the model. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for finding these features in LLMs, and it has been postulated that they can be used to find a \textit{canonical} set of units: a unique and complete list of atomic features. We cast doubt on this belief using two novel techniques: SAE stitching to show they are incomplete, and meta-SAEs to show they are not atomic. SAE stitching involves inserting or swapping latents from a larger SAE into a smaller one. Latents from the larger SAE can be divided into two categories: \emph{novel latents}, which improve performance when added to the smaller SAE, indicating they capture novel information, and \emph{reconstruction latents}, which can replace corresponding latents in the smaller SAE that have similar behavior. The existence of novel features indicates incompleteness of smaller SAEs. Using meta-SAEs -- SAEs trained on the decoder matrix of another SAE -- we find that latents in SAEs often decompose into combinations of latents from a smaller SAE, showing that larger SAE latents are not atomic. The resulting decompositions are often interpretable; e.g. a latent representing ``Einstein'' decomposes into ``scientist'', ``Germany'', and ``famous person''. Even if SAEs do not find canonical units of analysis, they may still be useful tools. We suggest that future research should either pursue different approaches for identifying such units, or pragmatically choose the SAE size suited to their task. We provide an interactive dashboard to explore meta-SAEs: https://metasaes.streamlit.app/

papers.title: Temporal Sparse Autoencoders: Leveraging the Sequential Nature of Language for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate temporal consistency into sparse autoencoders to better recover high-level semantic features in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs) that incorporate a temporal contrastive loss to encourage consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens, leading to better disentanglement of semantic and syntactic features in language models.
papers.conclusion: Temporal SAEs leverage the sequential nature of language to better extract semantic features, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.
papers.key_findings:
T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
T-SAEs exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal.
T-SAEs show improved disentanglement between high-level (semantic) and low-level (syntactic) features.
T-SAEs provide practical interpretability benefits, such as in safety monitoring and steering.
papers.abstract: Translating the internal representations and computations of models into concepts that humans can understand is a key goal of interpretability. While recent dictionary learning methods such as Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide a promising route to discover human-interpretable features, they suffer from a variety of problems, including a systematic failure to capture the rich conceptual information that drives linguistic understanding. Instead, they exhibit a bias towards shallow, token-specific, or noisy features, such as "the phrase 'The' at the start of sentences". In this work, we propose that this is due to a fundamental issue with how dictionary learning methods for LLMs are trained. Language itself has a rich, well-studied structure spanning syntax, semantics, and pragmatics; however, current unsupervised methods largely ignore this linguistic knowledge, leading to poor feature discovery that favors superficial patterns over meaningful concepts. We focus on a simple but important aspect of language: semantic content has long-range dependencies and tends to be smooth over a sequence, whereas syntactic information is much more local. Building on this insight, we introduce Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T-SAEs), which incorporate a novel contrastive loss encouraging consistent activations of high-level features over adjacent tokens. This simple yet powerful modification enables SAEs to disentangle semantic from syntactic features in a self-supervised manner. Across multiple datasets and models, T-SAEs recover smoother, more coherent semantic concepts without sacrificing reconstruction quality. Strikingly, they exhibit clear semantic structure despite being trained without explicit semantic signal, offering a new pathway for unsupervised interpretability in language models.

papers.title: Generalizing biological surround suppression based on center surround similarity via deep neural network models
papers.research_question: How do feedforward deep convolutional neural networks exhibit and generalize surround suppression effects based on center-surround similarity, and how do they compare to biological neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that feedforward convolutional neural networks exhibit surround suppression based on center-surround similarity, similar to biological V1 neurons, and introduces a gradient-based visualization method to generalize these effects to complex stimuli.
papers.conclusion: The findings generalize surround suppression to complex stimuli, providing testable hypotheses for higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach offers a new paradigm for biological experiments.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs show that the most suppressive surround orientation matches the center orientation, akin to V1 neurons.
Visualization reveals that for complex stimuli, the most suppressive surround is visually similar to the center.
In late layers, the most suppressive surround can follow changes in the center stimulus.
These effects are not present in untrained networks, indicating the role of learning.
Mismatches with biology include lack of geometric dependency in surround suppression and differences in contrast effects.
papers.limitation:
Feedforward CNNs lack clear center-surround separation and do not capture all biological surround effects, such as geometric dependencies.
CNNs show mismatches in contrast-dependent effects compared to cortical neurons.
future_direction: Elucidating the abstract mathematical form of surround effects in CNNs.
Incorporating scene statistics and divisive normalization into deep neural networks.
Testing hypotheses about efficient coding and high-order spatial dependencies.
papers.abstract: Sensory perception is dramatically influenced by the context. Models of contextual neural surround effects in vision have mostly accounted for Primary Visual Cortex (V1) data, via nonlinear computations such as divisive normalization. However, surround effects are not well understood within a hierarchy, for neurons with more complex stimulus selectivity beyond V1. We utilized feedforward deep convolutional neural networks and developed a gradient-based technique to visualize the most suppressive and excitatory surround. We found that deep neural networks exhibited a key signature of surround effects in V1, highlighting center stimuli that visually stand out from the surround and suppressing responses when the surround stimulus is similar to the center. We found that in some neurons, especially in late layers, when the center stimulus was altered, the most suppressive surround surprisingly can follow the change. Through the visualization approach, we generalized previous understanding of surround effects to more complex stimuli, in ways that have not been revealed in visual cortices. In contrast, the suppression based on center surround similarity was not observed in an untrained network. We identified further successes and mismatches of the feedforward CNNs to the biology. Our results provide a testable hypothesis of surround effects in higher visual cortices, and the visualization approach could be adopted in future biological experimental designs.

papers.title: Interpretable and Explainable Machine Learning for Materials Science and Chemistry
papers.research_question: How can interpretability and explainability techniques be applied to machine learning models in materials science and chemistry to improve scientific discovery, build trust, and unveil correlations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper summarizes applications of interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and chemistry, discussing how these techniques can improve scientific studies by providing insights beyond predictive power, building trust, and revealing unexpected correlations.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning is crucial for realizing the true potential of ML in materials science, and human experts who embrace interpretable ML will replace those who do not.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability in scientific machine learning involves trade-offs between explainability, completeness, and scientific validity (correctness).
Intrinsically interpretable models (e.g., linear models, decision trees) offer direct interpretations but may lack correctness for complex phenomena.
Extrinsic interpretation methods (e.g., SHAP, salience maps, attention mechanisms) can provide insights for complex models like deep neural networks.
Interpretability techniques can generate scientific hypotheses and guide experiments, but they require careful validation to avoid over-interpretation and confusion with causation.
Future directions include integrating uncertainty estimates into explanations and combining machine learning with causal inference for more robust insights.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability methods may lead to over-interpretation, especially when searching for physical explanations, and can be misled by shortcut learning or unrealistic feature combinations.
Explanations from machine learning models do not have strong causal guarantees and are susceptible to confounding effects, requiring secondary confirmation by experiments or simulation.
There is a trade-off between interpretability, completeness, and correctness in model explanations, meaning no single explanation may fully capture the model's operation and physical reality.
future_direction: Integrating uncertainty estimates into model explanations to improve confidence in insights.
Combining machine learning with causal inference to uncover cause-and-effect relationships from materials data.
Using advanced methods like autoencoders and sparse regression to directly extract physical knowledge from noisy experimental data.
papers.abstract:
While the uptake of data-driven approaches for materials science and
chemistry is at an exciting, early stage, to realise the true potential of
machine learning models for successful scientific discovery, they must have
qualities beyond purely predictive power. The predictions and inner workings of
models should provide a certain degree of explainability by human experts,
permitting the identification of potential model issues or limitations,
building trust on model predictions and unveiling unexpected correlations that
may lead to scientific insights. In this work, we summarize applications of
interpretability and explainability techniques for materials science and
chemistry and discuss how these techniques can improve the outcome of
scientific studies. We discuss various challenges for interpretable machine
learning in materials science and, more broadly, in scientific settings. In
particular, we emphasize the risks of inferring causation or reaching
generalization by purely interpreting machine learning models and the need of
uncertainty estimates for model explanations. Finally, we showcase a number of
exciting developments in other fields that could benefit interpretability in
material science and chemistry problems.

papers.title: Using Interpretability to Identify a Novel Class of Alzheimer's Biomarkers
papers.research_question: How does the Pleiades epigenetic foundation model detect Alzheimer's disease from blood samples, and what interpretability methods reveal about its decision-making to identify novel biomarkers?
papers.core_contribution: The blog demonstrates how interpretability of the Pleiades model identifies fragmentomics (DNA fragment length patterns) as a novel class of biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease, enabling an interpretable classifier that generalizes better than previous biomarkers on independent data.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability of foundation models like Pleiades can guide biomarker discovery by identifying novel signals such as fragmentomics, serving as a tool for hypothesis triage in scientific research.
papers.key_findings:
Pleiades encodes fragment length and methylation signals in its representations, with fragment length dominating disease classification decisions.
Sparse autoencoders and gradient attribution identified nine SAE features primarily encoding fragment length that drive the majority of classification performance.
Fragment length embeddings form a U-shaped manifold with privileged values like 167 bp, corresponding to biologically significant nucleosomal lengths.
A logistic regression model using only fragmentomic features achieved AUROC 0.78 on an independent cohort, outperforming methylation or cell type deconvolution features alone.
Combining fragmentomic features with methylation and cell type deconvolution improved performance to AUROC 0.84, and the classifier did not generalize to Parkinson's disease, indicating specificity for Alzheimer's.
papers.limitation:
Sample size and cohort diversity: analysis based on 81 patients from a single cohort, with limited demographic and geographic context, leading to wide confidence intervals.
Interpretability-to-biology gap: interpretability identifies features driving predictions but does not confirm if they reflect underlying disease biology or artifacts, requiring experimental validation.
future_direction: Validate findings in larger, more diverse cohorts.
Conduct experimental validation to establish biological causality of fragmentomic features.
Apply interpretability methods to other foundation models for hypothesis generation.
papers.abstract: How does the Pleiades epigenetic foundation model detect Alzheimer's disease from blood samples, and what interpretability methods reveal about its decision-making to identify novel biomarkers? The blog demonstrates how interpretability of the Pleiades model identifies fragmentomics (DNA fragment length patterns) as a novel class of biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease, enabling an interpretable classifier that generalizes better than previous biomarkers on independent data. Interpretability of foundation models like Pleiades can guide biomarker discovery by identifying novel signals such as fragmentomics, serving as a tool for hypothesis triage in scientific research.

papers.title: Net2Vec: Quantifying and Explaining How Concepts are Encoded by Filters in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent are individual filters sufficient to express a concept, and to what extent are filters shared between concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Net2Vec, a framework for learning concept embeddings aligned to filter activations, and uses it to show that concepts are encoded distributively across multiple filters and that filters are often shared among concepts.
papers.conclusion: Concepts are encoded distributively across filters and filters are shared among concepts; the Net2Vec framework provides a way to quantify and explain these relationships.
papers.key_findings:
Multiple filters are required to code for a concept in most cases.
Filters are not concept-specific and often help encode multiple concepts.
Filter embeddings better characterize the meaning of a representation and its relationship to other concepts compared to single filter activations.
Linear combinations of filters outperform single filters for segmentation and classification tasks.
The number of filters required to encode a concept varies by concept category and task.
papers.limitation:
The approach is limited by its linear nature.
Failure cases occur for concepts with very few training examples or very small objects.
future_direction: Explore non-linear ways concepts can be better aligned to the filter space.
papers.abstract: In an effort to understand the meaning of the intermediate representations captured by deep networks, recent papers have tried to associate specific semantic concepts to individual neural network filter responses, where interesting correlations are often found, largely by focusing on extremal filter responses. In this paper, we show that this approach can favor easy-to-interpret cases that are not necessarily representative of the average behavior of a representation. A more realistic but harder-to-study hypothesis is that semantic representations are distributed, and thus filters must be studied in conjunction. In order to investigate this idea while enabling systematic visualization and quantification of multiple filter responses, we introduce the Net2Vec framework, in which semantic concepts are mapped to vectorial embeddings based on corresponding filter responses. By studying such embeddings, we are able to show that 1., in most cases, multiple filters are required to code for a concept, that 2., often filters are not concept specific and help encode multiple concepts, and that 3., compared to single filter activations, filter embeddings are able to better characterize the meaning of a representation and its relationship to other concepts.

papers.title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations
papers.research_question: How do cognitive and expressive capabilities develop and interact in large language models across pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback stages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cognitive capabilities in LLMs are established during pretraining, while expressive capabilities develop during SFT and RLHF, with cognitive capability setting an upper bound for expressive capability.
papers.conclusion: This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of LLM training processes.
papers.key_findings:
Cognitive capability is primarily established during the pretraining stage, whereas expressive capability develops during SFT and RLHF.
There is a strong statistical correlation between cognitive and expressive capabilities, with cognitive capability acting as an upper bound.
The gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities can be bridged by optimization-free methods such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling.
The vocabulary linear layer plays a crucial role in expressive capability, and its training during SFT/RLHF helps reduce the gap.
Layer-wise analysis reveals a plateau in cognitive capability in deeper layers, indicating redundancy in the model architecture.
future_direction: Exploring additional linear analysis techniques for model analysis and control.
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model's cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model's capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs' architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

papers.title: This Looks Like That... Does it? Shortcomings of Latent Space Prototype Interpretability in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: Does the similarity in latent space used by prototype-based models correspond to human-interpretable similarity in input space? The paper investigates the semantic gap that can corrupt interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that prototype-based interpretability methods suffer from a semantic gap between latent space similarity and human-interpretable input space similarity, which can be corrupted by adversarial noise or compression artefacts.
papers.conclusion: Practitioners should be cautious when using prototype-based models, especially in sensitive domains like medical imaging, because the interpretability can break down in the presence of adversarial noise or compression artefacts.
papers.key_findings:
Small adversarial perturbations can cause ProtoPNet to identify prototypes in arbitrary, non-sensical locations while maintaining correct classification.
JPEG compression artefacts can cause ProtoPNet to assign drastically different similarity scores to visually similar image patches, breaking the interpretability.
The interpretability mechanism is not robust to common data corruptions.
Adversarial training and data augmentation can partially mitigate these issues but at the cost of accuracy.
future_direction: More comprehensive study of the robustness of interpretability mechanisms.
Examination of interpretable architectures different to ProtoPNets.
Identification of further sources of artefacts/noise that may lead to a break down of interpretability in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks that yield human interpretable decisions by architectural design have lately become an increasingly popular alternative to post hoc interpretation of traditional black-box models. Among these networks, the arguably most widespread approach is so-called prototype learning, where similarities to learned latent prototypes serve as the basis of classifying an unseen data point. In this work, we point to an important shortcoming of such approaches. Namely, there is a semantic gap between similarity in latent space and similarity in input space, which can corrupt interpretability. We design two experiments that exemplify this issue on the so-called ProtoPNet. Specifically, we find that this network's interpretability mechanism can be led astray by intentionally crafted or even JPEG compression artefacts, which can produce incomprehensible decisions. We argue that practitioners ought to have this shortcoming in mind when deploying prototype-based models in practice.

papers.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
papers.research_question: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? The paper proposes a benchmark to provide a basis for comparisons.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MIB, a benchmark for mechanistic interpretability with two tracks (circuit localization and causal variable localization) to enable meaningful comparisons of interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: MIB provides a standardized benchmark for comparing mechanistic interpretability methods, enabling meaningful evaluations and demonstrating progress in the field.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization.
Supervised Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) performs best on causal variable localization.
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are not better than non-featurized hidden vectors (neurons) for causal variable localization.
MIB enables meaningful comparisons and shows real progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The set of models and tasks is incomplete, limiting generalizability.
The metrics may not capture all aspects of interpretability that researchers care about.
The benchmark focuses on localization and featurization, leaving out other mechanistic interpretability goals like editing or control.
future_direction: Expand MIB to include more models and tasks.
Develop more comprehensive metrics that capture other aspects of interpretability.
Extend the benchmark to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components - and connections between them - most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable localization track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAE features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

papers.title: Towards Compositionality in Concept Learning
papers.research_question: How can we automatically discover compositional concept representations from foundation models, given that existing unsupervised concept extraction methods fail to produce composable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Compositional Concept Extraction (CCE), an unsupervised method that enforces orthogonality between concept attributes to extract compositional concept representations from foundation models, improving both compositionality and downstream task performance.
papers.conclusion: CCE successfully extracts compositional concept representations from foundation models, addressing the compositionality shortcomings of existing methods and enhancing downstream performance.
papers.key_findings:
Existing unsupervised concept extraction methods (e.g., PCA, ACE, Dictionary Learning) fail to produce compositional concept representations.
Ground-truth concept representations in foundation models (e.g., CLIP) are compositional, exhibiting orthogonality between attributes and non-orthogonality within attributes.
The proposed CCE method enforces these orthogonality properties by construction and extracts more compositional concepts than baselines across image and text datasets.
Concepts extracted by CCE yield better accuracy on downstream classification tasks compared to concepts from baseline methods.
The compositionality of concepts is vital for use cases like model explanation, behavior editing, and few-shot learning.
papers.limitation:
The study assumes concepts are compositional, but real-world concepts can be non-compositional (e.g., 'hot dog').
The concept structure is flat and does not account for hierarchical composition.
Unsupervised concept extraction requires manual inspection to assign names to discovered concepts, which can be labor-intensive.
future_direction: Study of non-compositional concepts.
Study of hierarchical concept structures.
papers.abstract: Concept-based interpretability methods offer a lens into the internals of foundation models by decomposing their embeddings into high-level concepts. These concept representations are most useful when they are compositional, meaning that the individual concepts compose to explain the full sample. We show that existing unsupervised concept extraction methods find concepts which are not compositional. To automatically discover compositional concept representations, we identify two salient properties of such representations, and propose Compositional Concept Extraction (CCE) for finding concepts which obey these properties. We evaluate CCE on five different datasets over image and text data. Our evaluation shows that CCE finds more compositional concept representations than baselines and yields better accuracy on four downstream classification tasks. Code and data are available at https://github.com/adaminsky/compositional_concepts .

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: From Words to Waves: Analyzing Concept Formation in Speech and Text-Based Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How do conceptual structures in speech models differ from those in text and multimodal models, and to what extent do different modalities yield shared or modality-specific semantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper compares conceptual structures in speech, text, and multimodal models, finding that text models directly encode linguistic taxonomies from early layers, while speech models gradually develop linguistic representations from acoustic features, and multimodal models exhibit unique alignment due to cross-modal training.
papers.conclusion: Text models directly encode linguistic structures from early layers, speech models gradually develop linguistic representations from acoustic features, and multimodal models show unique alignment patterns due to cross-modal training.
papers.key_findings:
Text models directly encode linguistic taxonomies from early layers, while speech models gradually transition from acoustic to linguistic representations.
Multimodal models like SpeechT5 exhibit unique alignment patterns due to cross-modal training.
Speech models allocate less capacity to linguistic and semantic taxonomies, focusing more on speech-specific features like phonetics.
Speech models show weaker performance in capturing negative sentiment compared to text models in task-specific tests.
papers.limitation:
Speech models struggle with tasks requiring deep linguistic reasoning compared to text-based models.
Speech-based sentiment classifiers have difficulty capturing negative sentiment effectively.
future_direction: Integrating additional linguistic or prosodic cues in speech-based models.
Leveraging multi-modal learning strategies.
Exploring alternative architectures to better capture nuances of spoken sentiment.
papers.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has demonstrated that systems trained solely on text can acquire extensive world knowledge, develop reasoning capabilities, and internalize abstract semantic concepts--showcasing properties that can be associated with general intelligence. This raises an intriguing question: Do such concepts emerge in models trained on other modalities, such as speech? Furthermore, when models are trained jointly on multiple modalities: Do they develop a richer, more structured semantic understanding? To explore this, we analyze the conceptual structures learned by speech and textual models both individually and jointly. We employ Latent Concept Analysis, an unsupervised method for uncovering and interpreting latent representations in neural networks, to examine how semantic abstractions form across modalities. For reproducibility we made scripts and other resources available to the community.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Low-$N$ Protein Function Prediction and Design
papers.research_question: How effective are sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for protein function prediction and design in low-data (low-N) regimes?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide a compact and biologically meaningful latent space that improves low-N fitness prediction and enables effective protein design via latent steering, outperforming ESM2 baselines.
papers.conclusion: SAEs are a powerful tool for low-N protein function prediction and design, expanding the biologist's toolkit for resource-constrained applications.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform ESM2 baselines in 58% of fitness extrapolation tasks with as few as 24 training sequences.
SAEs design top-fitness variants in 83% of cases via latent steering, compared to designing with ESM2 alone.
The sparse latent space of SAEs encodes biologically interpretable motifs and compresses relevant information, reducing overfitting in low-N regimes.
Analysis of steered variants reveals that SAEs activate latents corresponding to known biological motifs such as active sites, allosteric sites, and epistatic sites.
SAE performance is influenced by the number of available multiple sequence alignment (MSA) sequences for training.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to a set of proteins; it could be extended to other proteins with clinically relevant functions such as antibiotic resistance and viral replication.
SAE performance is strongly influenced by the number of MSA sequences available for training; strategies are needed for robust training when MSAs are shallow.
Protein engineering experiments rely on in-silico fitness models; wet lab validation is necessary to verify function.
Designed variants are constrained to a maximum of five mutations away from the wildtype; beyond this radius, designing highly-functional sequences is difficult with a single predictive latent.
In-silico evaluation tools become less reliable the further away variants are from the wildtype.
future_direction: Extend evaluation to other proteins with clinically relevant functions.
Explore strategies for robust SAE training when multiple sequence alignments are shallow or unavailable.
Couple SAE steering with physics-based tools like Rosetta to jointly optimize for both function and stability.
papers.abstract: Predicting protein function from amino acid sequence remains a central challenge in data-scarce (low-$N$) regimes, limiting machine learning-guided protein design when only small amounts of assay-labeled sequence-function data are available. Protein language models (pLMs) have advanced the field by providing evolutionary-informed embeddings and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled decomposition of these embeddings into interpretable latent variables that capture structural and functional features. However, the effectiveness of SAEs for low-$N$ function prediction and protein design has not been systematically studied. Herein, we evaluate SAEs trained on fine-tuned ESM2 embeddings across diverse fitness extrapolation and protein engineering tasks. We show that SAEs, with as few as 24 sequences, consistently outperform or compete with their ESM2 baselines in fitness prediction, indicating that their sparse latent space encodes compact and biologically meaningful representations that generalize more effectively from limited data. Moreover, steering predictive latents exploits biological motifs in pLM representations, yielding top-fitness variants in 83% of cases compared to designing with ESM2 alone.

papers.title: What Has a Foundation Model Found? Using Inductive Bias to Probe for World Models
papers.research_question: Does a foundation model's inductive bias align with a postulated world model, indicating that it has learned deeper structure from sequence prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an inductive bias probe to evaluate whether foundation models have learned a postulated world model, and finds that they often fail to do so, instead developing task-specific heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias probe reveals that foundation models often fail to learn the underlying world models, instead relying on task-specific heuristics, which limits their generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Foundation models trained on orbital trajectories fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks.
Models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.
In lattice and Othello, models have an inductive bias toward legal next-tokens rather than the world model.
Models that perform better on inductive bias probes have better transfer performance on new tasks that rely on the underlying world model.
LLMs also fail to predict force magnitudes accurately in physics tasks.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning proprietary LLMs is infeasible and running the full inductive bias probe is expensive.
papers.abstract: Foundation models are premised on the idea that sequence prediction can uncover deeper domain understanding, much like how Kepler's predictions of planetary motion later led to the discovery of Newtonian mechanics. However, evaluating whether these models truly capture deeper structure remains a challenge. We develop a technique for evaluating foundation models that examines how they adapt to synthetic datasets generated from some postulated world model. Our technique measures whether the foundation model's inductive bias aligns with the world model, and so we refer to it as an inductive bias probe. Across multiple domains, we find that foundation models can excel at their training tasks yet fail to develop inductive biases towards the underlying world model when adapted to new tasks. We particularly find that foundation models trained on orbital trajectories consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis reveals that these models behave as if they develop task-specific heuristics that fail to generalize.

papers.title: A Structured Dictionary Perspective on Implicit Neural Representations
papers.research_question: What is the expressive power of INRs? How does initialization affect their inductive bias?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a unified theoretical perspective on implicit neural representations (INRs), showing they are analogous to structured signal dictionaries with harmonics, and that their inductive bias is characterized by the neural tangent kernel (NTK), with meta-learning reshaping the NTK like dictionary learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes the expressive power and inductive bias of INRs from a unified perspective, showing harmonic expansion and NTK characterization, and reveals that meta-learning modifies the NTK to increase efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
INRs have expressive power equivalent to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the input mapping frequencies.
The frequency support of INRs grows exponentially with depth as each layer splits input into higher order harmonics.
INRs suffer from failure modes such as imperfect recovery and aliasing due to their harmonic expansion.
The inductive bias of INRs is captured by the ability of their empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) to encode target signals efficiently.
Meta-learning increases the encoding efficiency of the NTK by constructing a rich signal dictionary from combinations of meta-training tasks.
papers.limitation: Most practical results are performed using one or two-dimensional signals, and insights should be extensible to higher dimensions.
future_direction: Generalize Theorem 1 to input mappings beyond sinusoids or include normalization layers.
Study the effect of out-of-distribution data on the alignment with the NTK after meta-training.
Design methods to visualize the eigenfunctions of the NTK in higher dimensions.
papers.abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to classical discretized representations of signals. Nevertheless, despite their practical success, we still do not understand how INRs represent signals. We propose a novel unified perspective to theoretically analyse INRs. Leveraging results from harmonic analysis and deep learning theory, we show that most INR families are analogous to structured signal dictionaries whose atoms are integer harmonics of the set of initial mapping frequencies. This structure allows INRs to express signals with an exponentially increasing frequency support using a number of parameters that only grows linearly with depth. We also explore the inductive bias of INRs exploiting recent results about the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK). Specifically, we show that the eigenfunctions of the NTK can be seen as dictionary atoms whose inner product with the target signal determines the final performance of their reconstruction. In this regard, we reveal that meta-learning has a reshaping effect on the NTK analogous to dictionary learning, building dictionary atoms as a combination of the examples seen during meta-training. Our results permit to design and tune novel INR architectures, but can also be of interest for the wider deep learning theory community.

papers.title: Measuring the Interpretability of Unsupervised Representations via Quantized Reverse Probing
papers.research_question: How to measure the interpretability (semantics encoded) of self-supervised visual representations by estimating the mutual information between the representation and a space of manually labelled concepts via a decoding bottleneck.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to measure the interpretability of unsupervised representations by estimating mutual information between quantized representations and human-interpretable concepts via reverse linear probing, providing a single number sensitive to semanticity and the encoding of concept combinations.
papers.conclusion: Quantized reverse probing is an effective method for measuring the interpretability of self-supervised visual representations, revealing differences in semantic content across methods and providing qualitative insights into the learned concepts.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed interpretability measure ranks self-supervised methods differently than standard linear classification accuracy.
Clustering-based self-supervised methods generally produce more interpretable representations.
Interpretability increases when using Vision Transformer (ViT) backbones compared to ResNet-50.
The method can discover elementary concepts (objects, scenes, materials, textures) encoded in the representations, including combinations of attributes.
Longer pre-training does not always lead to more interpretable representations.
papers.abstract: Self-supervised visual representation learning has recently attracted significant research interest. While a common way to evaluate self-supervised representations is through transfer to various downstream tasks, we instead investigate the problem of measuring their interpretability, i.e. understanding the semantics encoded in raw representations. We formulate the latter as estimating the mutual information between the representation and a space of manually labelled concepts. To quantify this we introduce a decoding bottleneck: information must be captured by simple predictors, mapping concepts to clusters in representation space. This approach, which we call reverse linear probing, provides a single number sensitive to the semanticity of the representation. This measure is also able to detect when the representation contains combinations of concepts (e.g., "red apple") instead of just individual attributes ("red" and "apple" independently). Finally, we propose to use supervised classifiers to automatically label large datasets in order to enrich the space of concepts used for probing. We use our method to evaluate a large number of self-supervised representations, ranking them by interpretability, highlight the differences that emerge compared to the standard evaluation with linear probes and discuss several qualitative insights. Code at: {\scriptsize{\url{https://github.com/iro-cp/ssl-qrp}}}.

papers.title: Concept Activation Regions: A Generalized Framework For Concept-Based Explanations
papers.research_question: How can we provide concept-based explanations for deep neural networks without assuming linear separability of concept examples in the latent space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Regions (CARs), a generalized framework for concept-based explanations that relaxes the linear separability assumption of Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) by using kernel-based support vector classifiers.
papers.conclusion: CARs offer a more flexible and accurate framework for concept-based explanations, providing better descriptions of concept distributions, more human-consistent global explanations, and meaningful concept-based feature importance.
papers.key_findings:
CAR classifiers more accurately describe how concepts are scattered in the DNN's latent space compared to CAV classifiers.
CAR provides global explanations (TCAR scores) that are more consistent with human concept annotations than TCAV scores.
CAR enables concept-based feature importance that meaningfully relates concepts with each other.
CAR can be used to show that DNNs autonomously rediscover known scientific concepts, such as the prostate cancer grading system.
future_direction: Using CARs to analyze large-scale language models.
Exploring concept-based contrastive learning to improve explainability of shallow layers.
papers.abstract: Concept-based explanations permit to understand the predictions of a deep neural network (DNN) through the lens of concepts specified by users. Existing methods assume that the examples illustrating a concept are mapped in a fixed direction of the DNN's latent space. When this holds true, the concept can be represented by a concept activation vector (CAV) pointing in that direction. In this work, we propose to relax this assumption by allowing concept examples to be scattered across different clusters in the DNN's latent space. Each concept is then represented by a region of the DNN's latent space that includes these clusters and that we call concept activation region (CAR). To formalize this idea, we introduce an extension of the CAV formalism that is based on the kernel trick and support vector classifiers. This CAR formalism yields global concept-based explanations and local concept-based feature importance. We prove that CAR explanations built with radial kernels are invariant under latent space isometries. In this way, CAR assigns the same explanations to latent spaces that have the same geometry. We further demonstrate empirically that CARs offer (1) more accurate descriptions of how concepts are scattered in the DNN's latent space; (2) global explanations that are closer to human concept annotations and (3) concept-based feature importance that meaningfully relate concepts with each other. Finally, we use CARs to show that DNNs can autonomously rediscover known scientific concepts, such as the prostate cancer grading system.

papers.title: Unsupervised Interpretable Basis Extraction for Concept-Based Visual Explanations
papers.research_question: How can we extract an interpretable basis for the feature space of a CNN's intermediate layer without requiring supervised concept annotations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised, post-hoc method to extract an interpretable basis for CNN feature spaces by optimizing for a sparsity property that holds for interpretable bases, eliminating the need for concept annotations.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an unsupervised method for interpretable basis extraction that can improve the interpretability of CNN feature representations and reveals a limitation of supervised approaches (single direction per concept), suggesting directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed unsupervised method can extract bases that improve interpretability metrics (S1, S2) over the natural feature space basis.
In terms of the S1 metric, the unsupervised method can outperform a supervised baseline (IBD) because it can assign multiple basis directions to a single concept, covering different parts of the concept dataset.
In terms of the S2 metric, the unsupervised method underperforms the supervised baseline because assigning multiple directions to a concept limits the number of unique concepts the basis can describe.
The extracted bases are approximately orthogonal, supporting the hypothesis that interpretable bases should be orthogonal for independent and mutually exclusive concepts.
The method demonstrates applicability across standard CNN architectures (VGG16BN, ResNet18, AlexNet, GoogleNet) and training datasets (Places365, ImageNet).
papers.limitation:
The method may assign multiple basis directions to a single concept, which limits the number of different unique concepts that can be described by the basis.
The method does not handle positively correlated concepts (e.g., 'has-a' relationships) well, as it assumes orthogonality for independent and mutually exclusive concepts.
future_direction: Consider an approximately orthogonal and over-complete basis of the feature space (i.e., I > D) to overcome the limitation of assigning multiple directions to a single concept.
papers.abstract: An important line of research attempts to explain CNN image classifier predictions and intermediate layer representations in terms of human-understandable concepts. Previous work supports that deep representations are linearly separable with respect to their concept label, implying that the feature space has directions where intermediate representations may be projected onto, to become more understandable. These directions are called interpretable, and when considered as a set, they may form an interpretable feature space basis. Compared to previous top-down probing approaches which use concept annotations to identify the interpretable directions one at a time, in this work, we take a bottom-up approach, identifying the directions from the structure of the feature space, collectively, without relying on supervision from concept labels. Instead, we learn the directions by optimizing for a sparsity property that holds for any interpretable basis.
